children.title: Elementary Boolean Relations

children.title: Directional Implication Pair
children.top_down_role: Directional logical dependence and its converse.

children.title: Forward Implication
children.top_down_role: Directional dependence from an antecedent condition to a consequent condition.

assumptions_latex: \(y_p,y_q\in\{0,1\}\) are their truth indicators, with value \(1\) denoting true.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\Rightarrow q\iff y_p\le y_q\).

notation.meaning: Truth indicators of propositions p and q.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary linear representation of a single forward Boolean implication.

source_refs.locator: 4.5.1 A Disjunctive Programming Formulation p. 64

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Boolean propositions \(p\) and \(q\), the forward implication \(p\Rightarrow q\) excludes exactly the truth assignment \((y_p,y_q)=(1,0)\). Hence its exact binary linear representation is \[y_p\le y_q,\qquad y_p,y_q\in\{0,1\}.\] Equivalently, the implication is the disjunction \(\neg p\lor q\). The inequality imposes no restriction on \(y_q\) when \(y_p=0\), while it forces \(y_q=1\) when \(y_p=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forward implication is represented by ordering the antecedent's truth indicator below the consequent's indicator.
knowledge_statements.title: Forward Implication

source_witnesses.locator: 4.5.1 A Disjunctive Programming Formulation p. 64

children.title: Reverse Implication
children.top_down_role: Converse directional dependence relative to a designated implication.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\Rightarrow p\iff y_q\le y_p\).

notation.meaning: Truth indicators of propositions p and q.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary linear representation obtained by reversing antecedent and consequent.

source_refs.locator: 4.5.1 A Disjunctive Programming Formulation p. 64

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reverse implication associated with \(p\Rightarrow q\) is \(q\Rightarrow p\), not another expression of the original direction. It excludes exactly \((y_p,y_q)=(0,1)\) and has the exact binary linear representation \[y_q\le y_p,\qquad y_p,y_q\in\{0,1\}.\] Equivalently, it is \(\neg q\lor p\). Thus \(y_q=1\) forces \(y_p=1\), whereas \(y_q=0\) leaves \(y_p\) unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reversing an implication swaps antecedent and consequent, producing the opposite indicator inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Reverse Implication

source_witnesses.locator: 4.5.1 A Disjunctive Programming Formulation p. 64

children.title: Directional Asymmetry
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions between the two implication directions.

assumptions_latex: \(p\) and \(q\) are Boolean propositions with truth indicators \(y_p,y_q\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In general, \(p\Rightarrow q\not\Rightarrow q\Rightarrow p\).

notation.meaning: Truth indicators of propositions p and q.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-equivalence of the two directions of implication.

source_refs.locator: 4.5.1 A Disjunctive Programming Formulation p. 64

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The constraints representing the two implication directions are generally distinct: \(p\Rightarrow q\) requires \(y_p\le y_q\), whereas \(q\Rightarrow p\) requires \(y_q\le y_p\). The assignment \((y_p,y_q)=(0,1)\) satisfies the forward implication but violates the reverse implication; the assignment \((1,0)\) has the opposite behavior. Imposing both directions yields \(y_p=y_q\), which is logical equivalence and is strictly stronger than either direction alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One implication direction does not establish the other; enforcing both directions produces equivalence.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Asymmetry

source_witnesses.locator: 4.5.1 A Disjunctive Programming Formulation p. 64

children.title: Vacuous-Truth Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where inactive antecedents limit the information carried by an implication.

assumptions_latex: Material implication is interpreted by the classical truth table.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\Rightarrow q\) is true whenever \(p\) is false, independently of \(q\).

notation.meaning: Truth indicators of antecedent and consequent.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical vacuous truth and its formulation consequence.

source_refs.locator: 4.5.1 A Disjunctive Programming Formulation p. 64

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(p\Rightarrow q\) is equivalent to \(\neg p\lor q\), it is true for both assignments \((y_p,y_q)=(0,0)\) and \((0,1)\). In the representation \(y_p\le y_q\), setting \(y_p=0\) therefore imposes no restriction on \(y_q\). Consequently, an implication constraint alone cannot force its antecedent to hold, nor can observations made only when the antecedent is false determine the truth of its consequent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A false antecedent makes a material implication true and leaves the consequent unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.title: Vacuous-Truth Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 4.5.1 A Disjunctive Programming Formulation p. 64

children.title: Reified Equivalence Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Bidirectional connections between truth values and modeled conditions.

children.title: Logical Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Bidirectional correspondence between logical conditions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\Leftrightarrow q\iff y_p=y_q\).

notation.meaning: Truth indicators of the two propositions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact binary encoding of equivalence between two propositions.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.4 The smooth binary formulation p. 11
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Logical equivalence holds precisely when the two propositions have the same truth value. For binary truth indicators, \[p\Leftrightarrow q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y_p=y_q.\] Equivalently, one may impose the pair \(y_p\le y_q\) and \(y_q\le y_p\), representing \(p\Rightarrow q\) and \(q\Rightarrow p\), respectively. The feasible truth assignments are exactly \((y_p,y_q)=(0,0)\) and \((1,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two propositions are logically equivalent exactly when their binary truth indicators are equal.
knowledge_statements.title: Logical Equivalence

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.4 The smooth binary formulation p. 11
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

children.title: Constraint Reification
children.top_down_role: Truth-variable representations of modeled constraint status.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a prescribed domain and \(C(x)\) is a Boolean-valued constraint predicate on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b=1\iff C(x)\) holds.

notation.meaning: Boolean constraint predicate evaluated at x.
Binary variable reifying the truth of the constraint.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic definition of full constraint reification.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.2 Disjunctive constraints p. 10
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary variable \(b\) fully reifies a constraint predicate \(C(x)\) on \(X\) when, for every \(x\in X\), \[b=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C(x)\text{ is true}.\] Thus \(b=1\) requires \(C(x)\), and satisfaction of \(C(x)\) requires \(b=1\). Equivalently, \(b=0\) holds exactly when \(C(x)\) is false. This definition is semantic; a mixed-integer formulation must encode both implication directions exactly over the stated domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reified constraint has a binary variable equal to one exactly when the constraint is true.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Reification

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.2 Disjunctive constraints p. 10
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

children.title: Bidirectional Truth Linkage
children.top_down_role: Structural coupling between a truth indicator and a modeled condition.

assumptions_latex: \(C(x)\) is a decidable Boolean predicate on a domain \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((b=1\Rightarrow C(x))\land(C(x)\Rightarrow b=1)\iff b=1\Leftrightarrow C(x)\).

notation.meaning: Predicate whose truth is linked to the binary variable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete two-direction condition for exact truth linkage.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.4 The smooth binary formulation p. 11
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact truth linkage between \(b\) and \(C(x)\) requires both implications \[b=1\Rightarrow C(x),\qquad C(x)\Rightarrow b=1.\] Equivalently, it may be expressed as \(b=1\Rightarrow C(x)\) together with \(b=0\Rightarrow\neg C(x)\). Under these two directions, \(b=1\) exactly on the subset \(\{x\in X:C(x)\text{ is true}\}\), and \(b=0\) exactly on its complement in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact linkage requires both the indicator-to-constraint implication and the constraint-to-indicator implication.
knowledge_statements.title: Bidirectional Truth Linkage

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.4 The smooth binary formulation p. 11
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

children.title: Partial Reification Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where only one direction of a truth link is represented.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Reification Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of converse inference under one-way reification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The one-way constraint \(b=1\Rightarrow C(x)\) is only a partial reification. When \(C(x)\) is true, both \(b=0\) and \(b=1\) satisfy this implication, so satisfaction of \(C(x)\) does not imply \(b=1\), and \(b=0\) does not determine whether \(C(x)\) is true or false. Nevertheless, \(b=1\) does imply \(C(x)\). Conversely, the constraint \(C(x)\Rightarrow b=1\) permits \(b=1\) when \(C(x)\) is false. Omitting either implication direction therefore prevents exact truth correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single implication preserves one direction of inference but does not fully reify the constraint's truth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Satisfaction of \(C(x)\) need not imply \(b=1\).

children.title: Boolean Composition Duality
children.top_down_role: Composition of simultaneous and alternative logical conditions.

children.title: Conjunctive Composition
children.top_down_role: Composition of conditions that must hold simultaneously.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjunctive Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear formulation of a finite Boolean conjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary inputs \(y_1,\ldots,y_m\), a binary variable \(z\) equals their conjunction exactly when \[z\le y_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad z\ge\sum_{i=1}^m y_i-(m-1).\] The upper inequalities force \(z=0\) if any input is zero, while the lower inequality forces \(z=1\) when every input is one. Thus the feasible binary points satisfy \(z=1\) if and only if \(y_i=1\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conjunction indicator is bounded above by every input and below by their sum minus the number of excess inputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z=\bigwedge_{i=1}^m y_i\) exactly under the displayed inequalities.

notation.meaning: Binary truth indicator of the conjunction.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

children.title: Disjunctive Composition
children.top_down_role: Composition of conditions represented as alternatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear formulation of a finite Boolean disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary inputs \(y_1,\ldots,y_m\), a binary variable \(z\) equals their disjunction exactly when \[z\ge y_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad z\le\sum_{i=1}^m y_i.\] The lower inequalities force \(z=1\) if any input is one, while the upper inequality forces \(z=0\) when every input is zero. Thus the feasible binary points satisfy \(z=1\) if and only if \(y_i=1\) for at least one \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disjunction indicator is bounded below by every input and above by their sum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z=\bigvee_{i=1}^m y_i\) exactly under the displayed inequalities.

notation.meaning: Binary truth indicator of the disjunction.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

children.title: Nested Composition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Navigation for depth, duplication, and structural growth in nested logical compositions.

assumptions_latex: \(t\) is intended to represent \(y_1\land y_2\), and \(w\) is intended to represent \(t\lor y_3\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One-way inner-gate constraints need not represent the nested formula exactly.

notation.meaning: Auxiliary indicator for the inner conjunction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness boundary for auxiliary variables in nested Boolean formulations.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Nested composition is exact when every auxiliary gate is linked bidirectionally to its defining subformula. If the intended inner relation \(t=y_1\land y_2\) is replaced only by \(t\le y_1\) and \(t\le y_2\), exactness can fail even when the outer relation \(w=t\lor y_3\) is encoded exactly. Indeed, \((y_1,y_2,y_3,t,w)=(1,1,0,0,0)\) satisfies those constraints, although the true value of \((y_1\land y_2)\lor y_3\) is \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested formulation can be inexact when an auxiliary gate is constrained in only one direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested Composition Boundaries

children.title: Exclusive-Choice Parity Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Mutually exclusive, odd-parity, and even-parity logical structures.

children.title: Exclusive-Choice Relations
children.top_down_role: Selection structures permitting a designated exclusive alternative.

knowledge_statements.title: Exclusive-Choice Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the exactly-one relation for a finite family of Boolean variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For Boolean variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\{0,1\}\), with \(n\ge 1\), the exclusive-choice relation holds precisely when exactly one variable is true. Its binary linear representation is
\[
\operatorname{EXACTLYONE}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=1.
\]
For \(n=2\), this relation coincides with exclusive OR; for \(n>2\), it is stronger than odd parity because it excludes assignments having three or more true variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly one Boolean variable is true. For two variables this is XOR; for larger families it is stricter than requiring an odd number of true variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{EXACTLYONE}(x)\iff \sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=1\)

notation.meaning: Boolean truth indicator for alternative i

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exactly-one definition and its distinction from odd parity are mathematically correct, and definition fits this leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Odd-Parity Relations
children.top_down_role: Logical structures characterized by odd selected support.

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Parity Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes odd Boolean parity using an integer counting variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), the odd-parity relation holds exactly when the number of true components is odd. Equivalently,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=2k+1
\]
for some \(k\in\mathbb Z\) satisfying \(0\le k\le\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\). Thus the relation is the congruence \(\sum_i x_i\equiv 1\pmod 2\); unlike exclusive choice, it permits every odd positive cardinality not exceeding \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Odd parity requires an odd number of true variables. An integer auxiliary variable expresses the true-variable count as twice an integer plus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\equiv 1\pmod 2\iff \exists k\in\mathbb Z:\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=2k+1\)
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded integer characterization of odd parity is correct and condition fits the container, but the record has no source with a specific locator.

children.title: Even-Parity Relations
children.top_down_role: Logical structures characterized by even selected support.

knowledge_statements.title: Even-Parity Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes even Boolean parity using an integer counting variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), the even-parity relation holds exactly when the number of true components is even, including zero. Equivalently,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=2k
\]
for some \(k\in\mathbb Z\) satisfying \(0\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\). Hence the relation is the congruence \(\sum_i x_i\equiv 0\pmod 2\), and it is the Boolean complement of odd parity on the same variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even parity requires an even number of true variables, including zero. Its cardinality equals twice a bounded integer auxiliary variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\equiv 0\pmod 2\iff \exists k\in\mathbb Z:\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=2k\)
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The even-parity characterization, including the zero case and auxiliary-variable bounds, is correct, but no inspectable source is cited.

children.title: Parity Representation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural limits of direct versus extended parity representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Parity Representation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies why the parity-count auxiliary must retain integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the parity equation \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=2k+b\), where \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) and \(b\in\{0,1\}\) selects even or odd parity. If \(k\) is permitted to be continuous, then every binary assignment satisfies the equation by taking
\[
k=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i-b}{2}.
\]
Consequently, without integrality or another discrete parity description, the projected formulation imposes no parity restriction on \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing the parity-count variable to be continuous destroys the restriction: every binary assignment can choose a real count variable satisfying the equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k\in\mathbb R\Longrightarrow \operatorname{proj}_x\{(x,k):\sum_i x_i=2k+b\}=\{0,1\}^n\)

notation.meaning: desired parity bit, zero for even and one for odd

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The continuous-relaxation counterexample is correct and failure_boundary is the appropriate kind, but the claim lacks a cited source and locator.

children.title: Logical Normal Forms
children.top_down_role: Alternative organizations of logically equivalent models.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Elementary disjunctions and conjunctions; CNF and DNF
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite propositional formulas whose atomic statements are inequalities, equations, or systems of them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An elementary disjunction (respectively, elementary conjunction) is a disjunction (respectively, conjunction) whose terms contain no further disjunctions (respectively, conjunctions). A formula is in conjunctive normal form if it has the form \[\varphi_{\mathrm{CNF}}=\bigwedge_{i=1}^{m}\left(\bigvee_{j\in J_i}P_{ij}\right),\] and it is in disjunctive normal form if it has the form \[\varphi_{\mathrm{DNF}}=\bigvee_{k=1}^{r}\left(\bigwedge_{\ell\in K_k}Q_{k\ell}\right).\] An atomic statement is regarded as a degenerate elementary conjunction or disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An elementary disjunction has no disjunct containing a further disjunction, and an elementary conjunction has no conjunct containing a further conjunction. Conjunctive normal form is a conjunction of elementary disjunctions, while disjunctive normal form is a disjunction of elementary conjunctions. A single atomic inequality or equation counts as a degenerate elementary form.
assumptions_latex: \varphi\text{ is a finite propositional formula whose atomic statements are inequalities, equations, or systems thereof.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi_{\mathrm{CNF}}=\bigwedge_i\bigvee_{j\in J_i}P_{ij},\qquad \varphi_{\mathrm{DNF}}=\bigvee_k\bigwedge_{\ell\in K_k}Q_{k\ell}.

source_evidence.locator: Disjunctive Programming and Its Relation to Integer Programming / 1.3. Inequality Systems with Logical Connectives / Definition 1.3-extra-3

children.title: Conjunctive Normal-Form Models
children.top_down_role: Clause-centered organizations of logical restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjunctive Normal-Form Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents Boolean feasibility as an intersection of clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A Boolean formula is in conjunctive normal form when it has the representation
\[
F(x)=\bigwedge_{j=1}^{m}\left(\bigvee_{\ell\in C_j}\ell\right),
\]
where every \(C_j\) is a finite set of literals and each literal is either \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\). An assignment satisfies \(F\) exactly when every clause contains a satisfied literal. With binary variables, the clause \(\bigvee_{i\in P}x_i\vee\bigvee_{i\in N}\neg x_i\) is represented by \(\sum_{i\in P}x_i+\sum_{i\in N}(1-x_i)\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A CNF model is an intersection of clauses. Each clause requires at least one of its positive or negated Boolean literals to be true.
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_j\) is a finite nonempty literal set
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=1\iff \forall j,\ \bigvee_{\ell\in C_j}\ell=1\)

notation.meaning: indices of positive and negated literals in one clause

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

children.title: Disjunctive Normal-Form Models
children.top_down_role: Alternative-centered organizations exposing unions of feasible regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Normal-Form Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents Boolean feasibility as a union of conjunction-defined alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A Boolean formula is in disjunctive normal form when it has the representation
\[
F(x)=\bigvee_{r=1}^{q}\left(\bigwedge_{\ell\in T_r}\ell\right),
\]
where every \(T_r\) is a finite set of literals. An assignment satisfies \(F\) exactly when it satisfies every literal of at least one term. If term \(r\) also indexes a continuous feasible region \(P_r\), the corresponding disjunctive feasible set is the union \(\bigcup_{r=1}^{q}P_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DNF model is a union of alternatives, each described by a conjunction. Feasibility requires all literals of at least one alternative.
assumptions_latex: Each \(T_r\) is a finite literal set
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=1\iff \exists r:\bigwedge_{\ell\in T_r}\ell=1\)

notation.meaning: feasible region associated with alternative r

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

children.title: Regular Disjunctive Forms
children.top_down_role: Structured normal forms used for systematic disjunctive convexification.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Disjunctive Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a finite union of explicitly indexed conjunctive systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite disjunctive feasible set is in regular indexed form when each alternative is stated as one conjunctive system:
\[
S=\bigcup_{r=1}^{q}P_r,
\qquad
P_r=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A^r x\le b^r\}.
\]
Equivalently, membership is expressed by \(\bigvee_{r=1}^{q}[A^r x\le b^r]\), where the inequalities inside each bracket are conjoined. This form exposes every alternative separately and therefore permits alternative-wise convexification or mixed-integer encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular indexed disjunction writes the feasible set as a finite union of explicitly listed conjunctive systems, enabling separate treatment of each alternative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in S\iff \bigvee_{r=1}^{q}[A^r x\le b^r]\)

source_refs.locator: 4.5.1 A Disjunctive Programming Formulation p. 64

source_witnesses.locator: 4.5.1 A Disjunctive Programming Formulation p. 64

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Initial Hull-Relaxation Identity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The notation refers to the initial CNF regular form and associated polyhedron in the surrounding construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F_0=\bigcap_{j\in T_0}S_j be the initial CNF regular form and let P_0=\bigcap_{j\in T_0^*}S_j be its associated polyhedron. Then \operatorname{h-rel}F_0=P_0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the initial conjunctive-normal-form representation in the construction, its hull relaxation equals the associated polyhedron P0.
assumptions_latex: F_0=\bigcap_{j\in T_0}S_j\text{ is the specified initial CNF regular form}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular, Conjunctive, Disjunctive, and Improper Disjunctive Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and elementary implications for polyhedral disjunctive normal forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A disjunctive set is in regular form if
\[
F=\bigcap_{j\in T}S_j,\qquad S_j=\bigcup_{i\in Q_j}P_i,
\]
where every \(P_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a polyhedron. A regular form is in conjunctive normal form if every \(S_j\) is elementary, meaning every constituent \(P_i\) is a halfspace, and it is in disjunctive normal form if \(|T|=1\). Each \(S_j\) in a regular form is itself in disjunctive normal form. Such an \(S_j\) is improper if \(S_j=P_i\) for some \(i\in Q_j\), and proper otherwise. If \(|Q_j|=1\), then \(S_j\) is improper; every improper \(S_j\) is convex and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular-form disjunctive set is an intersection of unions of polyhedra. It is in conjunctive normal form when every constituent polyhedron is a halfspace and in disjunctive normal form when the intersection has one factor. Each factor is itself in disjunctive normal form. A factor is improper when it equals one of its constituent polyhedra and proper otherwise. A singleton union is improper, and every improper factor is convex and polyhedral.
assumptions_latex: P_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a polyhedron for every relevant }i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{CNF}\iff (\forall j)(\forall i\in Q_j)\,P_i\text{ is a halfspace},\qquad \operatorname{DNF}\iff |T|=1;\qquad S_j\text{ improper}\iff (\exists i\in Q_j)(S_j=P_i),\quad |Q_j|=1\Rightarrow S_j\text{ improper}\Rightarrow S_j\text{ is convex and polyhedral}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conversion of Regular Form to Disjunctive Normal Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise-distribution procedure converting a finite regular polyhedral disjunctive form to DNF while preserving regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
F=\bigcap_{j\in T}S_j,\qquad S_j=\bigcup_{i\in Q_j}P_i
\]
be a regular-form disjunctive set with finite nonempty \(T\). Then \(F\) can be brought to disjunctive normal form by \(|T|-1\) applications of the following regularity-preserving step: choose distinct \(k,l\in T\) and replace \(S_k\cap S_l\) by
\[
S_{kl}=\bigcup_{\substack{i\in Q_k\\ j\in Q_l}}(P_i\cap P_j).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular-form disjunctive set with finitely many intersection factors can be converted to disjunctive normal form using |T|−1 pairwise distribution steps. Each step replaces the intersection of two unions by the union of all pairwise intersections of their constituent polyhedra and preserves regular form.
assumptions_latex: P_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a polyhedron for every relevant }i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_k\cap S_l=\bigcup_{\substack{i\in Q_k\\ j\in Q_l}}(P_i\cap P_j),\qquad F\text{ can be brought to DNF by }|T|-1\text{ such regularity-preserving applications}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hull Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines componentwise convexification before intersection and distinguishes that operation from convexifying the complete intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F=\bigcap_{j\in T}S_j be a regular-form disjunctive set, where each S_j is a union of polyhedra. Define its hull relaxation by \operatorname{h-rel}F:=\bigcap_{j\in T}\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}S_j. Thus the individual sets S_j are convexified before their intersection is taken; this is a different construction from forming \operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}F.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a regular disjunctive set expressed as an intersection of unions of polyhedra, its hull relaxation is the intersection of the closed convex hulls of the individual union components. This convexifies each component before intersection, rather than convexifying the full intersection.

children.title: Normal-Form Conversion Routes
children.top_down_role: Structural routes between logical representations and normal forms.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Form Conversion Routes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives exact expansion routes to CNF or DNF without auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite propositional formula \(F\). First eliminate implications and biconditionals, then push negations to literals using De Morgan laws and remove double negations. For a CNF output, repeatedly apply \(A\vee(B\wedge C)\equiv(A\vee B)\wedge(A\vee C)\). For a DNF output, repeatedly apply \(A\wedge(B\vee C)\equiv(A\wedge B)\vee(A\wedge C)\). Stop when the requested outer connective contains only clauses or terms, respectively; delete duplicate literals and absorbed clauses or terms. Output the resulting formula, which is logically equivalent to \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalize connectives and negations, then distribute disjunction for CNF or conjunction for DNF until only clauses or terms remain; simplify duplicates and absorption.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{out}}\equiv F\), with \(F_{\mathrm{out}}\) in the requested normal form

children.title: Conjunctive Normal-Form Growth
children.top_down_role: Representation growth associated with conjunctive normal-form conversion.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjunctive Normal-Form Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhibits exponential CNF size under auxiliary-free distributive conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(m\ge1\), let
\[
F_m=\bigvee_{i=1}^{m}(a_i\wedge b_i),
\]
where all \(2m\) variables are distinct. Distributive conversion without auxiliary variables yields
\[
F_m\equiv\bigwedge_{s\in\{0,1\}^m}\left(\bigvee_{i=1}^{m}c_{i,s_i}\right),
\qquad c_{i,0}=a_i,\quad c_{i,1}=b_i.
\]
Thus a DNF containing \(m\) two-literal terms can require \(2^m\) distinct CNF clauses, each of width \(m\). Auxiliary-free CNF normalization therefore has exponential worst-case output size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disjunction of m two-literal conjunctions expands into 2^m CNF clauses, demonstrating exponential auxiliary-free CNF growth.
assumptions_latex: The variables \(a_i,b_i\) are pairwise distinct Boolean variables
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_m\) has \(2^m\) clauses in its distributed auxiliary-free CNF

notation.meaning: the selected literal from pair i

children.title: Structural Loss During Normalization
children.top_down_role: Loss of shared structure or compact organization during normalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural Loss During Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical normalization preserves truth values but not the original decomposition syntax.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Normal-form conversion is not an injective encoding of a formula's decomposition structure. For example,
\[
(a\wedge b)\vee(a\wedge c)\equiv a\wedge(b\vee c).
\]
Both expressions therefore have the same simplified CNF, namely \(a\wedge(b\vee c)\), although the first explicitly records two alternatives sharing \(a\) and the second records a conjunction containing one clause. Hence truth-equivalent normalization preserves the satisfying assignments but cannot, from the normalized formula alone, recover the original alternative grouping or common-subexpression structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent formulas with different alternative groupings can normalize identically. Normalization preserves feasible assignments but may erase the original decomposition and shared-subexpression structure.
assumptions_latex: Absorption and duplicate elimination are allowed during normalization
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(F_1)=N(F_2)\nRightarrow F_1\text{ and }F_2\text{ have identical decomposition structure}\)

notation.meaning: truth-equivalent formulas with different parse structures

children.title: Truth-Table Representations

knowledge_statements.title: Truth-Table Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a Boolean relation by enumerating all satisfying assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) be the satisfying rows of a Boolean relation. Its truth-table DNF is
\[
F_S(x)=\bigvee_{v\in S}\left(\bigwedge_{i:v_i=1}x_i\wedge\bigwedge_{i:v_i=0}\neg x_i\right).
\]
Then \(F_S(x)=1\) exactly when \(x\in S\). An equivalent selector formulation introduces \(y_v\in\{0,1\}\) and imposes \(\sum_{v\in S}y_v=1\) and \(x_i=\sum_{v\in S}v_i y_v\) for every \(i\), thereby selecting one satisfying row.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate all satisfying Boolean rows. Their minterms form an exact DNF, or binary selectors can choose one row and reconstruct every variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_S(x)=1\iff x\in S\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-hot representation of a finite Boolean feasible set; its continuous relaxation represents the convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(z\in\{0,1\}^n\), membership in \(P\) has the exact extended representation
\[
z=\sum_{p\in P}p\lambda_p,\qquad \sum_{p\in P}\lambda_p=1,\qquad \lambda_p\in\{0,1\}\quad(p\in P).
\]
Exactly one pattern is selected. If instead \(\lambda_p\ge 0\) for all \(p\in P\), the projection onto the \(z\)-space is \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Boolean vector is admissible exactly when it equals one enumerated pattern selected by one-hot variables; relaxing those selectors yields the convex hull of all patterns.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(P\leftarrow\varnothing\). Visit every pattern \(p\in\{0,1\}^n\) once, in any fixed order. If \(F(p)=1\), update \(P\leftarrow P\cup\{p\}\); otherwise leave \(P\) unchanged. Stop after all \(2^n\) patterns have been tested and output \(P\). The procedure uses exactly \(2^n\) predicate evaluations and stores \(|P|\) patterns unless output is streamed.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An explicit list of \(P_n\) stores \(n|P_n|\) Boolean pattern entries, up to representation overhead, and its one-hot formulation uses \(|P_n|\) selectors. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acyclic Boolean circuits used as compositional representations of logical feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A logical circuit model assigns each input node \(i\) the value \(y_i=x_i\in\{0,1\}\). For every noninput node \(v\), with ordered predecessor tuple \(\operatorname{pred}(v)=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)\), it imposes
\[
y_v=\phi_v(y_{u_1},\ldots,y_{u_k}),\qquad y_v\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Acyclicity gives a unique evaluation in topological order. The represented feasible set is \(\{x\in\{0,1\}^m:y_t=1\}\), where \(t\) is the output node.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A logical circuit is an acyclic graph of Boolean gates. Inputs determine every intermediate value in topological order, and an assignment is accepted when the output equals one.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An expression-graph model for \(e\) is a directed acyclic graph \(G_e\) whose leaves are variables or constants and whose internal node \(v\) is labeled by an operator \(\psi_v\). If its children are \(u_1,\ldots,u_k\), node values satisfy \(y_v=\psi_v(y_{u_1},\ldots,y_{u_k})\). Each syntactically identical shared subexpression may be represented by one node with multiple outgoing uses. Recursive evaluation makes the value at the root \(r\) equal to \(e(x)\); thus \(y_r=1\) represents satisfaction of \(e\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be an expression tree containing \(k\) pairwise disjoint copies of the same rooted subexpression tree \(S\), with \(|V(S)|=s\). Replace these copies by one copy of \(S\) whose root feeds all former parent uses. Because every copy computes the same deterministic Boolean function of the same inputs, the resulting directed acyclic graph computes the same root function as \(T\). Its node count is \(|V(T)|-(k-1)s\), before accounting for edge-storage conventions.

children.title: Intermediate-Node Granularity
children.top_down_role: Choices governing the amount of auxiliary logical decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Intermediate-Node Granularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient exactness condition for replacing fine logical nodes by coarser acyclic blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(e:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}\) have a finite acyclic block decomposition with root block \(r\). For each block \(b\), let \(\xi_b(x,y)\) denote its tuple of original-variable inputs and predecessor-block outputs, introduce \(y_b\in\{0,1\}\), and impose \(\bigl(\xi_b(x,y),y_b\bigr)\in R_b\), where \(R_b\) is exactly the graph of the Boolean function computed by block \(b\). If the root block computes \(e\), then
\[
\operatorname{proj}_x\left\{(x,y):\bigl(\xi_b(x,y),y_b\bigr)\in R_b\ \forall b,\ y_r=1\right\}=\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^m:e(x)=1\right\}.
\]
Thus a change of intermediate-node granularity preserves the represented satisfying set whenever the resulting quotient graph is acyclic and every replacement block relation is exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coarser or finer intermediate blocks preserve the satisfying assignments when the block dependency graph remains acyclic, every block exactly relates its boundary inputs to its output, and the root computes the original formula.
assumptions_latex: \(e:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}\) is a Boolean function with a finite acyclic block decomposition.
Each block relation is the exact graph of its Boolean input-output function, and the root block computes \(e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection of the block-extended formulation onto \(x\) is exactly \(\{x\in\{0,1\}^m:e(x)=1\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered, not necessarily reduced, binary decision diagrams for Boolean feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An ordered binary decision diagram is a rooted directed acyclic graph with terminals labeled \(0\) and \(1\). Every nonterminal node \(v\) is labeled by some \(x_i\) and has successors \(v^0\) and \(v^1\); variable indices strictly increase along each root-to-terminal path. For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), evaluation follows edge \(x_i\) at a node labeled \(x_i\). The represented function \(f(x)\) is the reached terminal label, and the represented feasible set is \(\{x:f(x)=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordered binary decision diagram branches on Boolean variables in a fixed order. Each assignment follows one path and is feasible exactly when that path reaches the one-terminal.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Decision Diagrams

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ordered, not necessarily reduced BDD definition is mathematically precise and fits the topic role, but no inspectable authoritative source is supplied.

children.title: Multivalued Decision Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Decision-diagram representations for variables with more than two states.

assumptions_latex: Each variable \(x_i\) has a finite domain \(D_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The diagram represents exactly the assignments whose unique labeled path reaches the accepting terminal.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: multivalued decision diagrams extend binary branching to finite variable domains
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered multivalued decision diagrams over finite, possibly nonbinary, variable domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A multivalued decision diagram is a rooted directed acyclic graph with rejecting and accepting terminals. A nonterminal node associated with \(x_i\) has, for each permitted value \(a\in D_i\), an outgoing edge labeled \(a\); tested variable indices increase along every path. For \(x\in\prod_{i=1}^nD_i\), evaluation follows the edge labeled \(x_i\) whenever \(x_i\) is tested. The represented set is
\[
S=\{x\in\textstyle\prod_{i=1}^nD_i:\text{evaluation reaches the accepting terminal}\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multivalued decision diagram branches on values from finite variable domains. An assignment is represented exactly when its value-labeled path reaches the accepting terminal.
knowledge_statements.title: Multivalued Decision Diagrams

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-domain generalization of an ordered decision diagram matches the leaf, but it lacks an authoritative citation establishing the stated convention.

children.title: Layered Decision Diagrams
children.top_down_role: Decision diagrams organized into sequential decision layers.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with a root and terminal nodes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every root-to-terminal path advances through strictly increasing layer indices, and a fully layered path selects one arc between each consecutive pair of layers.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: layered acyclic diagrams are defined by a node partition and forward arcs
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly layered decision diagrams with arcs only between consecutive layers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A layered decision diagram of depth \(n\) has a disjoint node partition \(V=V_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_n\), with the root in \(V_0\) and terminals in \(V_n\), and an arc partition \(A=A_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}A_{n-1}\), where \(A_i\subseteq V_i\times V_{i+1}\). Arc labels encode the decision made at stage \(i+1\). Consequently, every root-to-terminal path contains exactly one arc from each \(A_i\) and defines one sequential decision tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A layered decision diagram partitions nodes by stage and permits arcs only to the next stage, so each complete path records one decision at every stage.
knowledge_statements.title: Layered Decision Diagrams

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strict consecutive-layer definition and path consequence are coherent and correctly scoped, but no source is cited.

children.title: Nonbinary State Spaces
children.top_down_role: State organization for choices with multivalued domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonbinary State Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state semantics for sequential decisions with arbitrary finite domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q_0,\ldots,Q_n\) be finite state sets, let \(q_0\in Q_0\), and let \(\delta_i:Q_{i-1}\times D_i\rightharpoonup Q_i\) be a partial transition function for each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A sequence \(x\in\prod_{i=1}^n D_i\) induces states recursively by \(q_i=\delta_i(q_{i-1},x_i)\) whenever that transition is defined. For accepting states \(T\subseteq Q_n\), the represented set is
\[
S=\left\{x\in\prod_{i=1}^n D_i:q_i\text{ is defined for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\ q_n\in T\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonbinary decisions update a finite state stage by stage. A sequence is represented when every value-triggered transition exists and its final state is accepting.
assumptions_latex: For every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the decision domain \(D_i\) and state sets \(Q_{i-1},Q_i\) are finite.
The initial state satisfies \(q_0\in Q_0\), and \(T\subseteq Q_n\) is the accepting-state set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transition system represents exactly the sequences \(x\in\prod_{i=1}^nD_i\) whose induced transitions are all defined and terminate in \(T\).

notation.meaning: accepting states in the final layer

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-state transitions provide standard semantics for nonbinary sequential diagrams

children.title: Sequential Layer Structure
children.top_down_role: Ordering and connectivity regimes across diagram layers.

assumptions_latex: Variables are ordered as \((x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), with finite domains \(D_i\).
Each layer records equivalence classes of feasible prefixes having identical admissible completions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Root-to-accepting paths are in bijection with the represented feasible decision sequences.

notation.meaning: set of feasible completions of prefix \(u\)

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: residual-completion equivalence yields exact sequential state merging
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact layer semantics based on residual feasible-completion sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible set \(S\subseteq\prod_{j=1}^nD_j\), define the residual completion set of a prefix \(u\in\prod_{j=1}^iD_j\) by
\[
C_i(u)=\{w\in	extstyle\prod_{j=i+1}^nD_j:(u,w)\in S\}.
\]
Place prefixes \(u,v\) in the same layer-\(i\) state exactly when \(C_i(u)=C_i(v)\). From the state of \(u\), an arc labeled \(a\in D_{i+1}\) leads to the state of \((u,a)\) whenever \(C_{i+1}(u,a)\ne\varnothing\). Then accepting paths correspond bijectively to members of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each stage, prefixes with the same feasible completions may share a state. Labeled transitions extend prefixes, and accepting paths correspond exactly to feasible full sequences.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Layer Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Residual-completion equivalence gives a coherent exact layer-merging property and the content kind fits, but the construction and bijection claim have no inspectable citation.

children.title: Big-M Granularity Designs
children.top_down_role: Shared, constraint-specific, direction-specific, and alternative-specific activation bounds.

children.title: Single-M Designs
children.top_down_role: Activation formulations using a shared bound across multiple restrictions.

assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(I\) is a finite nonempty index set.
For each \(i\in I\), \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(b_i\in\mathbb{R}\), and the intended implication is \(z=1\Rightarrow a_i^\top x\le b_i\), where \(z\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any \(M\ge \sup_{x\in X}\max_{i\in I}(a_i^\top x-b_i)_+\) is valid, provided the supremum is finite.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A common constant shared by all inequalities controlled by one binary variable.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The single-\(M\) formulation is \[a_i^\top x\le b_i+M(1-z)\qquad(i\in I).\] It is valid on \(X\) whenever the finite constant \(M\) satisfies \[M\ge \sup_{x\in X}\max_{i\in I}(a_i^\top x-b_i)_+.\] At \(z=1\), the original inequalities are imposed; at \(z=0\), every point of \(X\) satisfies the relaxed inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-M design uses one finite constant for every controlled inequality, chosen to dominate the largest possible inactive-state violation.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-M Designs

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

children.title: Constraint-Specific M Designs
children.top_down_role: Activation bounds specialized to individual constraints.

assumptions_latex: For every \(i\in I\), \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(b_i\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(z=1\Rightarrow a_i^\top x\le b_i\), with \(z\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(M_i\ge M_i^*\) independently certifies row \(i\); if a common valid \(M\) is available, choosing \(M_i\in[M_i^*,M]\) cannot weaken the continuous relaxation relative to using \(M\) in every row.

notation.meaning: Big-M constant assigned to row i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate deactivation constants for individual activated constraint rows.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constraint-specific design is \[a_i^\top x\le b_i+M_i(1-z)\qquad(i\in I),\] where each row has its own constant. The smallest nonnegative valid value relative to \(X\) is \[M_i^*=\sup_{x\in X}(a_i^\top x-b_i)_+.\] Thus any \(M_i\ge M_i^*\) is valid. If \(M\) is a common valid constant, choosing \(M_i\in[M_i^*,M]\) for every \(i\in I\) cannot weaken the continuous relaxation relative to using \(M\) in every row.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each controlled inequality receives its own finite valid deactivation constant; constants no larger than a common valid value give a relaxation at least as strong as the common-M formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Specific M Designs

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

children.title: Direction-Specific M Designs
children.top_down_role: Activation bounds specialized to directional restriction families.

assumptions_latex: The activated requirement is \(z=1\Rightarrow g(x)=0\), where \(z\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Validity holds when \(M^+\ge\sup_{x\in X}g(x)_+\) and \(M^-\ge\sup_{x\in X}(-g(x))_+\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinct constants relax the upper and lower directions of an activated equality.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A direction-specific formulation of the activated equality is \[-M^-(1-z)\le g(x)\le M^+(1-z).\] It is valid on \(X\) provided \[M^+\ge\sup_{x\in X}g(x)_+\quad\text{and}\quad M^-\ge\sup_{x\in X}(-g(x))_+.\] At \(z=1\), both directions reduce to \(g(x)=0\); at \(z=0\), the constants independently cover the maximum positive and negative excursions of \(g\) on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An activated equality uses separate constants for positive and negative excursions, avoiding a shared constant determined by the worse direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Direction-Specific M Designs

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

children.title: Alternative-Specific M Designs
children.top_down_role: Activation bounds specialized to individual disjunctive alternatives.

assumptions_latex: Alternative \(k\) requires \(a_{ki}^\top x\le b_{ki}\) for every \(i\in I_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(M_{ki}\ge\sup_{x\in X}(a_{ki}^\top x-b_{ki})_+\) yields a valid alternative-indexed formulation.

notation.meaning: Deactivation constant for row i of alternative k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constants are indexed by the disjunctive alternative whose constraints they deactivate.

source_refs.locator: Generalized disjunctive programming: A framework for formulation and alternative algorithms for MINLP optimization p. 93
2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The alternative-specific big-\(M\) formulation is \[a_{ki}^\top x\le b_{ki}+M_{ki}(1-z_k)\qquad(k\in K,\ i\in I_k).\] For each alternative and row, validity on \(X\) follows from \[M_{ki}\ge\sup_{x\in X}(a_{ki}^\top x-b_{ki})_+.\] Because \(z_k=1\) selects alternative \(k\), its constraints are enforced without relaxation, while constraints belonging to every unselected alternative receive their own certified relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every alternative’s constraints receive separately indexed constants; selecting an alternative removes relaxation from precisely its rows.
knowledge_statements.title: Alternative-Specific M Designs

children.title: M-Value Certification
children.top_down_role: Routes for establishing valid finite activation bounds.

children.title: Domain-Based M Certification
children.top_down_role: Certification from explicit domains and local model structure.

assumptions_latex: The activated affine inequality is \(z=1\Rightarrow a^\top x\le b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_{\mathrm{box}}=\left(\sum_j a_j\widehat{x}_j-b\right)_+\) is a valid deactivation constant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form certification for affine rows over an explicit bounded box.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\widehat{x}_j=u_j\) when \(a_j\ge0\), and \(\widehat{x}_j=\ell_j\) when \(a_j<0\). Then \[\max_{x\in X}a^\top x=\sum_{j=1}^n a_j\widehat{x}_j,\] so the computable value \[M_{\mathrm{box}}=\left(\sum_{j=1}^n a_j\widehat{x}_j-b\right)_+\] certifies the validity of \(a^\top x\le b+M_{\mathrm{box}}(1-z)\). Any additional valid domain restriction may replace \(X\) and can only decrease the exact required constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an affine row over finite variable bounds, maximizing each coefficient at its appropriate endpoint gives a directly checkable valid M.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Based M Certification

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

children.title: Optimization-Based M Certification
children.top_down_role: Certification through auxiliary relaxation or subproblem analysis.

assumptions_latex: The activated inequality is \(z=1\Rightarrow g(x)\le0\), with \(z\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(U\in\mathbb{R}\) is a certified upper bound satisfying \(U\ge\sup_{x\in X}g(x)\), then \(M=\max\{0,U\}\) is a finite valid deactivation constant.

notation.meaning: Finite certified upper bound on the auxiliary maximization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certification by solving or bounding an auxiliary worst-violation problem.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. Convex and Lagrangian Relaxations p. 21
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the auxiliary value \[M^*=\sup\{g(x)_+:x\in X\}.\] If \(M^*<\infty\), it is the smallest nonnegative constant for which \[g(x)\le M^*(1-z)\] is valid on \(X\). More generally, any finite certified upper bound \(U\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(U\ge\sup_{x\in X}g(x)\) yields the valid choice \(M=\max\{0,U\}\). If \(M^*=+infty\), no finite deactivation constant is valid on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximizing the inactive row violation gives the smallest valid M when the value is finite; any finite certified upper bound also supplies a valid M, while an unbounded violation admits no finite M.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-Based M Certification

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

children.title: Disjunct-Local M Strengthening
children.top_down_role: Refinement using information local to alternatives and interacting restrictions.

assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), \(K\) is a finite nonempty set, and \(X_j\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is the feasible region of alternative \(j\in K\).
The variables satisfy \(z_j\in\{0,1\}\), \(\sum_{j\in K}z_j=1\), and \(z_j=1\Rightarrow x\in X_j\) for every \(j\in K\).
For each \(k\in K\), \(g_k:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), and selecting alternative \(k\) requires \(g_k(x)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite constants \(M_{kj}\ge\sup_{x\in X_j}g_k(x)_+\) for \(j\ne k\) validate \(g_k(x)\le\sum_{j\in K\setminus\{k\}}M_{kj}z_j\).

notation.meaning: Feasible set local to alternative j
Violation bound for row k when alternative j is selected

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inactive bounds are refined using the particular alternative that is active.

source_refs.locator: Generalized disjunctive programming: A framework for formulation and alternative algorithms for MINLP optimization p. 93
2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each ordered pair \((k,j)\) with \(j\ne k\), suppose the finite constant \(M_{kj}\) satisfies \[M_{kj}\ge\sup_{x\in X_j}g_k(x)_+.\] Then the disjunct-local formulation \[g_k(x)\le\sum_{j\in K\setminus\{k\}}M_{kj}z_j\qquad(k\in K)\] is valid. At \(z_k=1\), the right-hand side is zero; at \(z_j=1\) with \(j\ne k\), the right-hand side uses the bound certified on \(X_j\). Replacing all \(M_{kj}\) by a common valid bound no smaller than them cannot strengthen the continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When selection of alternative j implies membership in its local feasible region, an inactive row for alternative k can use a violation bound certified specifically on that region.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjunct-Local M Strengthening

children.title: Big-M Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Validity, relaxation, and numerical boundaries of bound-dependent encodings.

children.title: Missing or Invalid Activation Bounds
children.top_down_role: Unavailable finite bounds and incorrectly certified constants.

assumptions_latex: The implication is \(z=1\Rightarrow g(x)\le0\), and the proposed formulation is \(g(x)\le M(1-z)\), with \(z\in\{0,1\}\) and \(M\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite valid \(M\) exists if and only if \(V:=\sup_{x\in X}g(x)_+<infty\), and a finite \(M\) is valid if and only if \(M\ge V\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact validity boundary for existence and correctness of a finite activation constant.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[V:=\sup_{x\in X}g(x)_+.\] A finite deactivation constant exists on \(X\) if and only if \(V<infty\). For any finite \(M\ge0\), the formulation \[g(x)\le M(1-z)\] is valid for the implication on \(X\) if and only if \(M\ge V\). Thus \(V=+infty\) is the boundary for missing finite activation bounds, while \(M<V\) characterizes an invalid underestimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite valid M exists exactly when inactive violations are bounded, and a proposed finite M is valid exactly when it is at least the worst inactive violation.
knowledge_statements.title: Missing or Invalid Activation Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

children.title: Weak Big-M Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Relaxation degradation caused by permissive activation bounds.

assumptions_latex: The activation row is \(x\le Mz\), and the objective is to minimize \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integer optimum is \(1\), the continuous-relaxation optimum is \(1/M\), and their ratio is \(M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-row family exhibiting relaxation degradation proportional to the chosen constant.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(M\ge1\), consider the integer model \[\min\{z:x=1,\ x\le Mz,\ z\in\{0,1\}\}.\] Its optimum is \(1\). The relaxation obtained by replacing \(z\in\{0,1\}\) with \(0\le z\le1\) has optimum \(1/M\). The ratio of the integer optimum to the relaxation optimum is \(M\), so this family has arbitrarily weak relaxations as \(M\to+infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This one-row family has integer value one and relaxation value 1/M, producing an integer-to-relaxation ratio of M.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Big-M Relaxations

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

children.title: Big-M Numerical Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Finite-precision and conditioning effects associated with large coefficients.

children.title: Big-M Scaling Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Numerical effects caused by poorly scaled activation coefficients.

assumptions_latex: A row is represented as \(a^\top x+Mz\le b+M\), with at least one nonzero component of \(a\).
The row is used without coefficient rescaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Its nonzero coefficient dynamic range is at least \(M/\min_{j:a_j\ne0}|a_j|\) whenever \(M\ge\max_j|a_j|\).

notation.meaning: Smallest magnitude among ordinary nonzero row coefficients

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient-scale disparity introduced directly by a large activation constant.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the row \(a^\top x+Mz\le b+M\), define the nonzero coefficient dynamic range by \[\rho=\frac{\max\{M,\max_j|a_j|\}}{\min\bigl(\{M\}\cup\{|a_j|:a_j\ne0\}\bigr)}.\] If \(M\ge\max_j|a_j|\), then \(\rho\ge M/a_{\min}\), where \(a_{\min}=\min_{j:a_j\ne0}|a_j|\). Moreover, a perturbation \(\delta z\) changes the row activity by \(M\delta z\). Hence increasing \(M\) can create unbounded coefficient disparity and proportional activity amplification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A large M directly enlarges a row’s coefficient range and multiplies indicator perturbations, creating a clear scaling boundary for numerical reliability.
knowledge_statements.title: Big-M Scaling Pathologies

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coefficient-range identity is algebraically checkable, but the cited general big-M section does not establish a numerical scaling pathology or a reliability boundary. An authoritative numerical optimization or solver source with a specific locator is required before the exact terminal claim can be assessed.

children.title: Feasibility-Tolerance Leakage
children.top_down_role: Residual activity or constraint violation hidden within feasibility tolerances.

assumptions_latex: A numerical checker accepts it when its positive residual is at most \(\tau_f\max\{1,\|a\|_\infty,M,|b+M|\}\), where \(\tau_f>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(z=1\), accepted points may violate \(a^\top x\le b\) by up to \(\tau_f\max\{1,\|a\|_\infty,M,|b+M|\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional leakage bound under an explicitly stated scaled-residual acceptance rule.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[S=\max\{1,\|a\|_\infty,M,|b+M|\}.\] Under the stated numerical acceptance rule, a point is accepted whenever \[(a^\top x+Mz-b-M)_+\le\tau_f S.\] If \(z=1\), this becomes \[(a^\top x-b)_+\le\tau_f S.\] Consequently, although exact arithmetic enforces \(a^\top x\le b\), the numerical test permits an activated-row violation as large as \(\tau_f S\), which can grow proportionally with \(M\) under this scaling convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a scaled residual test, the accepted violation of an activated row can grow with M even when the indicator is exactly one.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Tolerance Leakage

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.3 Big-M constraints p. 11
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional residual calculation is correct under the stipulated acceptance rule, but no cited source supports that particular scaling convention or its use by a numerical checker. Because the leaf concerns an actual feasibility-tolerance pathology rather than a purely hypothetical rule, a solver or numerical-analysis source with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Integrality-Tolerance Leakage
children.top_down_role: Activation ambiguity associated with near-integral control variables.

assumptions_latex: The row is \(g(x)\le M(1-z)\), with intended binary indicator \(z\).
A solver treats every \(z\ge1-\tau_I\) as integral at value \(1\), where \(0<\tau_I<1\).

children.title: Conditioning Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Coefficient regimes where activation formulations become numerically fragile.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-precision boundary for a big-M activation row.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the activation row \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b+M(1-z)\), with \(z\in\{0,1\}\). Under floating-point rounding to nearest, changes in its right-hand side smaller than approximately \(\tfrac12\operatorname{ulp}(M)\) may be lost when \(z=0\). Moreover, the row dynamic range \(\rho=\max\{|a_i|,|b|,|M|:\text{nonzero}\}/\min\{|a_i|,|b|,|M|:\text{nonzero}\}\) grows at least proportionally to \(M\) when the other nonzero coefficients remain fixed. Thus excessively large valid values of \(M\) can make logically relevant residuals numerically indistinguishable and the relaxation poorly scaled, even though exact-arithmetic validity is preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid but excessively large big-M can overwhelm relevant residuals at machine precision and create an increasingly ill-scaled constraint row.
assumptions_latex: \(M>0\) is finite and the arithmetic uses finite-precision rounding to nearest.
At least one coefficient among \(a\) and \(b\) is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Large \(M\) can cross a finite-precision resolution and scaling boundary without changing exact-arithmetic logic.

notation.meaning: spacing between adjacent floating-point numbers near M
dynamic range of the nonzero row data

children.title: One-Way Indicator Constraints
children.top_down_role: Directional activation of modeled restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Way Indicator Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional implication from a binary truth value to one modeled restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in\{0,1\}\), let \(x\in X\), and let \(g:X\to\mathbb R\). The one-way indicator constraint \(z=1\Rightarrow g(x)\le0\) admits exactly those pairs \((x,z)\) for which either \(z=0\), with no restriction on \(g(x)\), or \(z=1\) and \(g(x)\le0\). It does not impose the converse implication: a feasible point with \(g(x)\le0\) need not have \(z=1\). An indicator triggered by \(z=0\) is obtained by replacing \(z\) with \(1-z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-way indicator enforces a constraint when its binary trigger is active, but satisfaction of the constraint does not force the trigger active.
assumptions_latex: \(g:X\to\mathbb R\) is defined on the modeled domain \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,z)\) is feasible exactly when \(z=0\) or \(g(x)\le0\).

children.title: Reified Constraint Families
children.top_down_role: Bidirectional correspondence between truth decisions and restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Reified Constraint Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bidirectional truth encoding for a scalar restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in\{0,1\}\), \(x\in X\), and \(g:X\to\mathbb R\). A reification of \(g(x)\le0\) is the equivalence \(z=1\Longleftrightarrow g(x)\le0\), comprising both \(z=1\Rightarrow g(x)\le0\) and \(g(x)\le0\Rightarrow z=1\). Equivalently, \(z=0\) must certify the logical negation \(g(x)>0\). In mixed-integer models using only non-strict inequalities, that negation requires a declared separation convention, such as \(g(x)\ge\varepsilon\) for a specified \(\varepsilon>0\); without such a convention, boundary points cannot be assigned an exact complementary inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reification makes a binary variable exactly represent a constraint’s truth value; encoding the false side requires an explicit convention for strict violation.
assumptions_latex: A false-state separation convention is specified when strict inequalities are unavailable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z=1\) holds exactly when \(g(x)\le0\) holds.

notation.meaning: declared positive separation for the false state

children.title: Indicator Reformulation Routes
children.top_down_role: Compilation into bound-based, extended, or disjunctive representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Reformulation Routes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent compilation routes for a binary-triggered feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z=1\Rightarrow g(x)\le0\) on \(x\in X\), the feasible set is \(S=(X\times\{0\})\cup(\{x\in X:g(x)\le0\}\times\{1\})\). If \(M\ge\sup_{x\in X}g(x)\), the inequality \(g(x)\le M(1-z)\) is an exact big-M representation for binary \(z\). Alternatively, one may retain the two-term disjunction directly. When both terms are bounded polyhedra, disaggregated variables and perspective scaling yield an extended convex-hull formulation whose continuous relaxation projects to \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\). These routes are integer-feasibility equivalent under their stated validity assumptions, but their relaxations and numerical behavior can differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indicator can compile to a valid big-M inequality, remain a disjunction, or use an extended convex-hull formulation; these routes differ in relaxation quality.
assumptions_latex: The big-M route uses a finite valid upper bound on \(g\) over \(X\).
The stated convex-hull route assumes bounded polyhedral disjuncts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each valid route represents \(S\) at integer \(z\), while the convex-hull route projects to \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\).

notation.meaning: valid upper bound on inactive-state violation

children.title: Native Indicator Processing
children.top_down_role: Presolve, propagation, branching, and strengthening that retain indicator identity.

knowledge_statements.title: Native Indicator Processing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-side processing that preserves indicator identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a model containing \(z=1\Rightarrow a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\), variable bounds, and an incumbent tolerance policy. At each search node, propagate bounds and fixings first. If \(z\) is fixed to \(1\), activate the row; if the row is impossible under current bounds, infer \(z=0\) or declare infeasibility when \(z=1\). If \(z\) is unfixed, use the implication for domain propagation, branching, or locally valid cuts without requiring a global oversized constant. Stop when the node is pruned or processed, and return updated domains, generated cuts, or child nodes while retaining the logical indicator metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Native processing propagates, branches, and generates cuts from an indicator directly, activating its row only when the trigger is fixed on.
assumptions_latex: The solver supports native indicator semantics and sound bound propagation.
All feasibility and integrality tolerances are fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output preserves validity of \(z=1\Rightarrow a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) while exploiting its logical identity during search.

children.title: Binary Product Linearizations

children.title: Fortet Binary-Product Linearizations
children.top_down_role: Classical representations of products among binary decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Fortet Binary-Product Linearizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ideal linear representation of the product of two binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in\{0,1\}\), introduce \(w\in\mathbb R\). Then \(w=xy\) is represented exactly by \(w\le x\), \(w\le y\), \(w\ge x+y-1\), and \(w\ge0\). For binary \(x\) and \(y\), these inequalities force \(w\in\{0,1\}\), so an explicit integrality declaration for \(w\) is unnecessary. If instead \(0\le x\le1\) and \(0\le y\le1\), the same system describes the convex hull of \(\{(x,y,w):x,y\in\{0,1\},\ w=xy\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four Fortet inequalities exactly linearize the product of two binaries and give the convex hull after relaxing the original binaries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities are equivalent to \(w=xy\) and form the binary-product convex hull.

children.title: Binary–Continuous Product Linearizations
children.top_down_role: Bound-dependent representations of products between binary and bounded continuous variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary–Continuous Product Linearizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact bound-dependent linearization of one binary–continuous product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in\{0,1\}\), \(L\le x\le U\), and introduce \(w\in\mathbb R\). The identity \(w=zx\) is represented exactly by \(Lz\le w\le Uz\), \(w\ge x-U(1-z)\), and \(w\le x-L(1-z)\). When \(z=0\), the first pair forces \(w=0\); when \(z=1\), the second pair forces \(w=x\). With \(0\le z\le1\), these inequalities describe the convex hull of the bounded graph \(\{(x,z,w):L\le x\le U,\ z\in\{0,1\},\ w=zx\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four bound-dependent inequalities exactly represent a binary times a bounded continuous variable and yield its convex hull relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities are equivalent to \(w=zx\) and give the bounded graph's convex hull when \(z\) is relaxed.

notation.meaning: valid finite bounds on the continuous factor

children.title: Multilinear Logical Liftings
children.top_down_role: Recursive and direct liftings for higher-order logical products.

knowledge_statements.title: Multilinear Logical Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct and recursive linear liftings of a binary conjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\) with \(k\ge2\), the product \(w=\prod_{i=1}^k x_i\) has the direct linear representation \(0\le w\), \(w\le x_i\) for every \(i\), and \(w\ge\sum_{i=1}^k x_i-k+1\). These inequalities force \(w=1\) exactly when every factor equals \(1\). A recursive lifting instead sets \(w_2=x_1x_2\) and \(w_j=w_{j-1}x_j\) for \(j=3,\ldots,k\), applying the two-factor Fortet inequalities at each stage. Both constructions are exact for binary factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary multilinear product can be linearized directly as an AND constraint or recursively through pairwise Fortet product variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either lifting enforces \(w=\prod_{i=1}^k x_i\) exactly.

children.title: Semi-Continuous Domains

knowledge_statements.title: Semi-Continuous Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-or-interval domain controlled by a binary activation variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given finite constants \(0<L\le U\), a semi-continuous variable \(x\) has domain \(\{0\}\cup[L,U]\): it is either inactive at zero or active within the closed interval \([L,U]\). Introducing \(z\in\{0,1\}\), this domain is represented by \(Lz\le x\le Uz\). The value \(z=0\) forces \(x=0\), while \(z=1\) forces \(L\le x\le U\). The positive lower bound distinguishes the active regime from the inactive state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semi-continuous variable is either exactly zero or lies in a prescribed nonzero interval, represented using one binary activation variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\{0\}\cup[L,U]\) if and only if some \(z\in\{0,1\}\) satisfies \(Lz\le x\le Uz\).

knowledge_statements.title: Semi-Integer Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-or-bounded-integer domain controlled by binary activation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given finite constants \(1\le L\le U\), a semi-integer variable \(x\) has domain \(\{0\}\cup(\mathbb Z\cap[L,U])\): it is either inactive at zero or an integer in the active interval. Introducing \(z\in\{0,1\}\), the domain is represented by \(x\in\mathbb Z\) together with \(Lz\le x\le Uz\). The value \(z=0\) forces \(x=0\), whereas \(z=1\) restricts \(x\) to the integer points between the active bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semi-integer variable is zero when inactive and otherwise takes an integer value between specified active bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\{0\}\cup(\mathbb Z\cap[L,U])\) if and only if \(x\in\mathbb Z\) and some \(z\in\{0,1\}\) satisfies \(Lz\le x\le Uz\).
