children.title: Inactive-State Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric role of the isolated inactive state.

knowledge_statements.title: Inactive-State Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of the zero state in a bounded on-off set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and define \(S=(\{0\}\times\{0\})\cup(C\times\{1\})\), with coordinates \((x,z)\). Then \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(x,z):0\le z\le1,\ x\in zC\}\), where \(zC=\{zy:y\in C\}\). Compactness implies \(0C=\{0\}\), so the slice at \(z=0\) contains only \(x=0\). If the active set is unbounded, the closed convex hull can instead contain nonzero recession directions at \(z=0\), and the singleton inactive-state description requires additional recession control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded convex active set, perspective scaling makes the inactive slice exactly the origin; unbounded active geometry may introduce recession directions there.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(x,z):0\le z\le1,\ x\in zC\}\) and its \(z=0\) slice is \(\{(0,0)\}\).

children.title: Active-Regime Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound and upper-bound structure governing the active regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Regime Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and tightness conditions for scalar on-off bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb R\) be the nonempty set of admissible active values of \(x\), and let \(z\in\{0,1\}\) select inactivity or activity. The inequalities \(Lz\le x\le Uz\) are valid for every point satisfying \(x=0\) when \(z=0\) and \(x\in D\) when \(z=1\) if and only if \(D\subseteq[L,U]\). These inequalities alone represent the on-off set exactly only when \(D=[L,U]\); otherwise additional constraints must describe membership in \(D\) in the active state. If \(\inf D\) and \(\sup D\) are finite, the tightest finite scalar bounds are \(L^*=\inf D\) and \(U^*=\sup D\). Replacing them by smaller lower bounds or larger upper bounds preserves validity but weakens the continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On-off bounds are valid exactly when their interval contains every active value. The active set’s finite infimum and supremum give the tightest scalar bounds, but the bounds alone describe an arbitrary active set exactly only when that set is the whole interval.
assumptions_latex: Finite scalar bounds are sought for the active values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Validity is equivalent to \(D\subseteq[L,U]\); when finite, \(L^*=\inf D\) and \(U^*=\sup D\) are the tightest scalar bounds.

notation.meaning: tightest finite active lower and upper bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Variable Upper-Bound Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary activation of bounded nonnegative modeled quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite index set, let \(y\in\{0,1\}\), and let \(u_i\in\mathbb{R}_+\) for every \(i\in I\). A variable upper-bound structure is the system \[0\le x_i\le u_i y\qquad(i\in I).\] Consequently, \(y=0\) forces \(x=0\), while \(y=1\) permits each component to range over \([0,u_i]\). If a positive activated lower bound is required, the corresponding semi-continuous form is \(\ell_i y\le x_i\le u_i y\), where \(0<\ell_i\le u_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary activity variable forces bounded quantities to zero when inactive and releases their prescribed componentwise bounds when active.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\ell_i\le u_i<\infty\) whenever an activated lower bound is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y=0\Rightarrow x=0\), and \(y=1\Rightarrow 0\le x_i\le u_i\) for all \(i\in I\).

notation.meaning: valid activated upper bound for component i

knowledge_statements.title: Activated Linear Subsystems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded linear subsystems switched by one binary variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:Av\le b\}\) be a nonempty bounded polyhedron and let \(z\in\{0,1\}\). The activated subsystem is represented by \[x\in zP,\] equivalently by \[Ax\le bz,\qquad z\in\{0,1\}.\] Boundedness of \(P\) ensures that \(\{x:Ax\le0\}=\{0\}\); hence \(z=0\) forces \(x=0\). When \(z=1\), the inequalities reduce to \(Ax\le b\), so the original linear subsystem is present.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling a bounded polyhedron by a binary variable yields zero when inactive and restores the original linear subsystem when active.

notation.meaning: scaled set consisting of vectors zv with v in P

children.title: Activated Convex Functions
children.top_down_role: Conditional convex costs and restrictions viewed through on–off geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Activated Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact binary on-off epigraph and its closed-perspective relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex, with \(0\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(f(0)=0\). Define its closed perspective by \[f^{\pi}(x,z)=\begin{cases}z f(x/z),&z>0,\\ f^{\infty}(x),&z=0,\\ +\infty,&z<0.\end{cases}\] For binary \(z\in\{0,1\}\), the constraints \(t\ge f^{\pi}(x,z)\) and \(z=0\Rightarrow x=0\) represent the on-off epigraph: the inactive state satisfies \(x=0\) and \(t\ge0\), while the active state satisfies \(t\ge f(x)\). Replacing binary membership by \(0\le z\le1\) and imposing \(t\ge f^{\pi}(x,z)\) gives the closed-perspective convex relaxation; its \(z=0\) slice satisfies \(t\ge f^{\infty}(x)\) and may contain nonzero recession directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For binary activation, the perspective inequality together with the inactive-state condition gives the exact on-off epigraph. Allowing activation between zero and one gives the closed-perspective convex relaxation, whose zero-activation boundary can include recession directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For binary \(z\), \(z=0\Rightarrow(x=0,\ t\ge0)\) and \(z=1\Rightarrow t\ge f(x)\); for \(0\le z\le1\), the closed-perspective relaxation is \(t\ge f^{\pi}(x,z)\).

knowledge_statements.title: At-Most-One Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary cardinality regime permitting zero or one selected item.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite index set and let \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) indicate selection of item \(i\). The vector \(y\) satisfies an at-most-one selection requirement precisely when \[\sum_{i\in I}y_i\le1.\] Thus its support \(\operatorname{supp}(y)=\{i\in I:y_i=1\}\) has cardinality at most one. The all-zero vector is feasible, so this regime permits making no selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At most one binary indicator may equal one; selecting no item remains feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert\operatorname{supp}(y)\rvert\le1\).

notation.meaning: indicator that item i is selected

knowledge_statements.title: Exactly-One Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary cardinality regime requiring a unique selected item.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite index set and let \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) indicate selection of item \(i\). knowledge_statements.title: Mutual-Exclusion Groups
knowledge_statements.scope_note: At-most-one constraints imposed separately on specified groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite index set, let \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq2^I\) be a family of nonempty groups, and let \(y\in\{0,1\}^{I}\). The selections satisfy groupwise mutual exclusion exactly when \[\sum_{i\in G}y_i\le1\qquad(G\in\mathcal{G}).\] Equivalently, no two selected indices occur together in any group: for all distinct \(i,j\in I\), if some \(G\in\mathcal{G}\) contains both, then \(y_i+y_j\le1\). Groups may overlap unless a partition is explicitly required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each specified group permits at most one selected member; overlapping groups induce additional pairwise incompatibilities.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{G}\) is a family of nonempty subsets of \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert G\cap\operatorname{supp}(y)\rvert\le1\) for every \(G\in\mathcal{G}\).

children.title: Unique-Choice Feasibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural cases where required unique selection conflicts with availability.

knowledge_statements.title: Unique-Choice Feasibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility distinction between optional and mandatory unique choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be finite and associate each alternative \(i\in I\) with a feasible set \(X_i\). A unique-choice disjunction requires \(y\in\{0,1\}^{I}\), \(\sum_{i\in I}y_i=1\), and membership in the selected \(X_i\). It is feasible if and only if \[\bigcup_{i\in I}X_i\ne\varnothing.\] Thus feasibility fails when \(I=\varnothing\) or every \(X_i\) is empty. Replacing equality by \(\sum_i y_i\le1\) admits the no-choice state and removes this failure only when that state satisfies all remaining constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mandatory unique choice is feasible exactly when at least one alternative is feasible; optional choice additionally admits the all-zero state.
assumptions_latex: Each \(X_i\) denotes the complete feasible set of alternative \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{exactly-one feasibility}\Longleftrightarrow\bigcup_{i\in I}X_i\ne\varnothing\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary feasibility boundary for finite disjunctions
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The elementary feasibility boundary is plausible and the failure-boundary kind fits, but no source is supplied. The sets X_i must also be declared subsets of a common decision space so that their union and selected membership are well-defined.

children.title: Cardinality Bound Classes
children.top_down_role: Upper, lower, interval, and fixed support-size restrictions.

children.title: Upper-Bounded Cardinality
children.top_down_role: Support-size restrictions governed by an upper limit.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Bounded Cardinality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite binary support constrained by an upper quota.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite index set, let \(y\in\{0,1\}^{I}\), and let \(U\) be an integer. An upper-bounded cardinality requirement is \[\sum_{i\in I}y_i\le U.\] It is equivalent to \(\lvert\operatorname{supp}(y)\rvert\le U\). Without other restrictions, the system is feasible exactly when \(U\ge0\); the inequality is redundant when \(U\ge\lvert I\rvert\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The number of selected binary items cannot exceed an integer upper quota.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert\operatorname{supp}(y)\rvert\le U\).

notation.meaning: set of indices having value one

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bounded Cardinality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite binary support constrained by a lower quota.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite index set, let \(y\in\{0,1\}^{I}\), and let \(L\) be an integer. A lower-bounded cardinality requirement is \[\sum_{i\in I}y_i\ge L.\] It is equivalent to \(\lvert\operatorname{supp}(y)\rvert\ge L\). Without other restrictions, the system is feasible exactly when \(L\le\lvert I\rvert\); the inequality is redundant when \(L\le0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The number of selected binary items must reach an integer lower quota.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert\operatorname{supp}(y)\rvert\ge L\).

children.title: Interval-Bounded Cardinality
children.top_down_role: Support-size restrictions confined to a specified interval.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval-Bounded Cardinality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite binary support constrained between two quotas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite index set, let \(y\in\{0,1\}^{I}\), and let \(L,U\in\mathbb{Z}\). An interval-bounded cardinality requirement is \[L\le\sum_{i\in I}y_i\le U.\] Equivalently, \(L\le\lvert\operatorname{supp}(y)\rvert\le U\). Without other restrictions, it is feasible exactly when \(\max\{0,L\}\le\min\{U,\lvert I\rvert\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The number of selected binary items must lie within an integer interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\le\lvert\operatorname{supp}(y)\rvert\le U\).

children.title: Exact Cardinality
children.top_down_role: Support-size restrictions requiring a fixed number of selected elements.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Cardinality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite binary support required to have prescribed size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite index set, let \(y\in\{0,1\}^{I}\), and let \(K\) be an integer. An exact-cardinality requirement is \[\sum_{i\in I}y_i=K.\] It is equivalent to \(\lvert\operatorname{supp}(y)\rvert=K\), or to imposing both lower and upper cardinality bounds with \(L=U=K\). Without other restrictions, it is feasible exactly when \(0\le K\le\lvert I\rvert\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly K binary items must be selected; feasibility requires K to lie between zero and the number of available items.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert\operatorname{supp}(y)\rvert=K\).

children.title: Grouped Cardinality Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Cardinality restrictions over grouped, nested, or overlapping selections.

children.title: Group Cardinality
children.top_down_role: Cardinality restrictions applied within designated groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Group Cardinality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate cardinality bounds assigned to specified index groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be finite, let \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq2^I\) be a family of nonempty groups, and let \(y\in\{0,1\}^{I}\). A group-cardinality system assigns integers \(L_G,U_G\) to each \(G\in\mathcal{G}\) and imposes \[L_G\le\sum_{i\in G}y_i\le U_G\qquad(G\in\mathcal{G}).\] Thus every group contains between \(L_G\) and \(U_G\) selected indices. No partition assumption is inherent: disjoint, nested, or overlapping families are obtained by restricting the incidence pattern of \(\mathcal{G}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each specified group receives its own lower and upper bound on the number of selected members.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{G}\) is a family of nonempty subsets of \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_G\le\lvert G\cap\operatorname{supp}(y)\rvert\le U_G\) for every \(G\in\mathcal{G}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard indexed family of cardinality bounds

children.title: Partitioned Cardinality
children.top_down_role: Cardinality restrictions organized over disjoint partitions.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite index set partitioned as \(I=G_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}G_m\).
\(x\in\{0,1\}^{I}\), and \(0\leq \ell_j\leq u_j\leq |G_j|\) are integers for every \(j\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses separate lower and upper selection bounds on every block of a partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be finite and let \(I=G_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}G_m\) be a partition. For a binary selection vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{I}\), choose integers \(\ell_j,u_j\) satisfying \(0\leq \ell_j\leq u_j\leq |G_j|\). A partitioned cardinality constraint is the system
\[
\ell_j\leq \sum_{i\in G_j}x_i\leq u_j,\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.
\]
Because the groups are disjoint, each selected index contributes to exactly one block count. One-sided and exact block cardinalities arise by omitting one bound or imposing \(\ell_j=u_j\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partitioned cardinality constraint bounds, separately, the number of selected items in each disjoint block of a finite ground set.

children.title: Nested-Group Cardinality
children.top_down_role: Cardinality restrictions organized over nested group systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested-Group Cardinality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers cardinality bounds on a chain of nested groups; branching laminar families require a constraint for each relevant group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be finite, let \(G_1\subsetneq G_2\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq G_m\subseteq I\), and let \(x\in\{0,1\}^{I}\). Define \(c_j=\sum_{i\in G_j}x_i\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\). Given integers \(0\leq \ell_j\leq u_j\leq |G_j|\), a nested-group cardinality system is
\[
\ell_j\leq c_j\leq u_j,\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.
\]
The nested sets give \(c_1\leq c_2\leq\cdots\leq c_m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested-group cardinality bounds the selected-item count in each set of a nested chain; the resulting counts are nondecreasing along the chain.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite index set and \(G_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq G_m\subseteq I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nested-group cardinality system is \(\ell_j\leq\sum_{i\in G_j}x_i\leq u_j\) for every \(j=1,\ldots,m\), and its counts satisfy \(c_1\leq\cdots\leq c_m\).

children.title: Overlapping-Group Cardinality
children.top_down_role: Cardinality restrictions over groups sharing selected elements.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite and \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\subseteq I\) may intersect.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) satisfies overlapping-group cardinality limits exactly when \(\ell_j\leq\sum_{i\in G_j}x_i\leq u_j\) for every group \(j\).
review_flags: target-specific authoritative source locator is absent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts selected items independently within groups that need not be disjoint or nested.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be finite and let \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\subseteq I\) be an arbitrary family, allowing \(G_j\cap G_k\neq\varnothing\). Given \(x\in\{0,1\}^{I}\) and integers \(0\leq\ell_j\leq u_j\leq |G_j|\), an overlapping-group cardinality system is
\[
\ell_j\leq\sum_{i\in G_j}x_i\leq u_j,\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.
\]
An item belonging to several groups contributes to every corresponding group count. Thus the constraints are coupled through shared variables, and no decomposition into independent group subproblems follows merely from their cardinality form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Overlapping-group cardinality bounds each group’s selected-item count while allowing an item to contribute simultaneously to several group counts.

children.title: Weighted Threshold Cardinality
children.top_down_role: Weighted logical sums and threshold structures.

children.title: Weighted Cardinality
children.top_down_role: Support restrictions based on weighted selected elements.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite, \(x\in\{0,1\}^{I}\), and \(w_i\geq0\) for all \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible selections are exactly \(\{x\in\{0,1\}^{I}:L\leq\sum_{i\in I}w_i x_i\leq U\}\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative contribution or size of item i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard nonnegative-weight form; arbitrary signed weights are treated separately.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be finite, let \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) indicate selection, and assign each item a weight \(w_i\geq0\). Define the weighted cardinality by
\[
W(x)=\sum_{i\in I}w_i x_i.
\]
For prescribed \(L,U\in\mathbb{R}\) with \(L\leq U\), a weighted cardinality constraint requires \(L\leq W(x)\leq U\). An upper-only, lower-only, or exact weighted cardinality constraint is obtained by retaining \(W(x)\leq U\), retaining \(W(x)\geq L\), or setting \(L=U\), respectively. Ordinary cardinality is the special case \(w_i=1\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted cardinality replaces the number of selected items by the sum of their nonnegative weights and constrains that sum between prescribed bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Cardinality

children.title: Threshold Constraints
children.top_down_role: Logical restrictions governed by attainment of a weighted threshold.

knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines binary linear threshold predicates under lower-threshold and upper-threshold conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be finite, \(x\in\{0,1\}^{I}\), \(a\in\mathbb{R}^{I}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}\). A lower-threshold constraint is
\[
a^{\mathsf T}x=\sum_{i\in I}a_i x_i\geq b,
\]
and an upper-threshold constraint uses \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq b\). The associated Boolean threshold function has value \(1\) exactly on the binary vectors satisfying the selected inequality. If \(a_i=1\) for every \(i\), the predicate is an ordinary cardinality bound; if the coefficients are nonnegative, it is a weighted-cardinality threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A threshold constraint classifies a binary vector according to whether its linear score is above or below a specified threshold; nonnegative coefficients give weighted-cardinality thresholds.
assumptions_latex: \(b\in\mathbb{R}\), and either the lower-threshold or upper-threshold convention is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted vectors are exactly those satisfying either \(a^{\mathsf T}x\geq b\) or \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq b\), according to the fixed convention.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

children.title: Pseudo-Boolean Threshold Structure
children.top_down_role: Threshold organization for weighted binary expressions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The threshold relation is a pseudo-Boolean constraint whose satisfaction set is \(\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\geq b\}\).
review_flags: target-specific authoritative source locator is absent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the integer-coefficient lower-threshold convention for pseudo-Boolean constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For Boolean variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\{0,1\}\), integer coefficients \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), and an integer threshold \(b\), the pseudo-Boolean threshold relation is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i x_i\geq b.
\]
Equivalently, it is the Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) defined by \(f(x)=1\) if and only if the displayed inequality holds. Integer data are without loss for rational coefficients and threshold after multiplication by a common positive denominator. Complementing or negating the comparison yields equivalent upper-threshold conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudo-Boolean threshold relation is an integer-weighted inequality over Boolean variables, equivalently a Boolean function determined by a linear threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Boolean Threshold Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The integer-coefficient pseudo-Boolean representation is standard and fits the leaf, but its normalization and equivalence claims require an inspectable authoritative source.

children.title: Weight-Sign Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions arising from nonnegative, mixed-sign, or signed weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Sign Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies coordinate effects and sufficient global monotonicity regimes by coefficient sign, with zero coefficients omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be finite and consider the predicate
\[
\sum_{i\in I}a_i x_i\geq b,
\qquad x\in\{0,1\}^{I},
\]
where \(a_i\neq0\) for every \(i\in I\). Define \(I^+=\{i\in I:a_i>0\}\) and \(I^-=\{i\in I:a_i<0\}\). A coordinate in \(I^+\) has a nondecreasing effect on satisfaction, while a coordinate in \(I^-\) has a nonincreasing effect. If \(I^-=\varnothing\), the predicate is monotone nondecreasing in the product order. If \(I^+=\varnothing\), it is monotone nonincreasing. With both signs present, neither global monotonicity conclusion follows in general; constant predicates and inessential coordinates are possible exceptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive coefficients make their coordinates increasing, negative coefficients make them decreasing, and uniform signs guarantee the corresponding global monotonicity. Mixed signs do not determine global monotonicity without further assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite, \(x\in\{0,1\}^{I}\), and \(a_i\neq0\) for every \(i\in I\).
The threshold predicate is \(\sum_{i\in I}a_i x_i\geq b\), with \(b\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive coefficients give nondecreasing coordinate effects, negative coefficients give nonincreasing coordinate effects, and uniform coefficient signs provide the corresponding sufficient global monotonicity regimes.

children.title: Cardinality Representation Families
children.top_down_role: Direct and extended representations with distinct size and inference properties.

children.title: Direct Linear Cardinality Models
children.top_down_role: Compact representations using original selection variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Direct Linear Cardinality Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact binary linear representation using only the original selection variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be finite and let \(x\in\{0,1\}^{I}\). Then
\[
|\operatorname{supp}(x)|=\sum_{i\in I}x_i.
\]
For integers \(L,U\) satisfying \(0\leq L\leq U\leq|I|\), the cardinality restriction \(L\leq|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\leq U\) has the direct linear representation
\[
L\leq\sum_{i\in I}x_i\leq U.
\]
No auxiliary variables are required. For an integer \(k\) with \(0\leq k\leq|I|\), at-most, at-least, and exactly \(k\) restrictions use \((L,U)=(0,k)\), \((L,U)=(k,|I|)\), and \((L,U)=(k,k)\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite binary selection vector, support size equals the sum of its entries, so cardinality bounds have a direct linear representation without auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system \(L\leq\sum_{i\in I}x_i\leq U\) represents \(L\leq|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\leq U\) without auxiliary variables.

children.title: Sequential Count-State Representations
children.top_down_role: Sequential-state and arithmetic representations of selection counts.

children.title: Counter Models
children.top_down_role: Sequential representations tracking discrete support counts.

knowledge_statements.title: Counter Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential finite-state counter representation for an at-most cardinality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\{0,1\}\) and let \(U\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\). Use states \(c_i\in\{0,ldots,U,\omega\}\), where \(\omega\) is an overflow state. Set \(c_0=0\) and, for \(i=1,\ldots,n\), apply
\[
c_i=
\begin{cases}
c_{i-1}+x_i, & c_{i-1}\neq\omega\text{ and }c_{i-1}+x_i\leq U,\\
\omega, & c_{i-1}=\omega\text{ or }c_{i-1}+x_i>U.
\end{cases}
\]
The counter accepts exactly when \(c_n\neq\omega\), which is equivalent to \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\leq U\). Allowed transitions may be encoded using binary state or arc variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A counter model processes binary decisions sequentially, stores the running count up to an upper limit, and enters a persistent overflow state when that limit is exceeded.
assumptions_latex: \(U\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), and \(\omega\) denotes a persistent overflow state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The counter accepts exactly the vectors satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\leq U\).

notation.meaning: counter state after processing the first i variables
state representing counts greater than U

review_flags: target-specific authoritative source locator is absent

children.title: Accumulator Models
children.top_down_role: Arithmetic-state representations tracking cumulative selected weight or count.

knowledge_statements.title: Accumulator Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear running-sum formulation with integer accumulator variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\{0,1\}\). Introduce integer variables \(s_0,\ldots,s_n\) and impose
\[
s_0=0,\qquad s_i=s_{i-1}+x_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).
\]
These equations define \(s_i=\sum_{t=1}^{i}x_t\), so \(s_n=\sum_{t=1}^{n}x_t\). For integers \(0\leq L\leq U\leq n\), the terminal bounds \(L\leq s_n\leq U\) represent \(L\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\leq U\). The prefix bounds \(0\leq s_i\leq i\) are valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accumulator models use integer running-sum variables linked by linear recurrences; bounds on the terminal accumulator exactly impose bounds on total cardinality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recurrence gives \(s_n=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\), so \(L\leq s_n\leq U\) exactly represents the stated cardinality bounds.

children.title: Sequential Count States
children.top_down_role: State organization across an ordered sequence of selection decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Count States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact, untruncated count states for a layered sequential representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\{0,1\}\). Define
\[
q_0=0,\qquad q_i=\sum_{t=1}^{i}x_t\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).
\]
The reachable state set at layer \(i\) is \(Q_i=\{0,1,\ldots,i\}\). From \(q\in Q_{i-1}\), the decision \(x_i=0\) gives the transition \(q\to q\), and \(x_i=1\) gives \(q\to q+1\). For any set \(K\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\), the terminal condition \(q_n\in K\) is equivalent to \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\in K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential count states record each exact prefix sum; a zero decision preserves the state, while a one decision increases it by one.
assumptions_latex: At layer \(i\), the state records the number selected among positions \(1,\ldots,i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reachable states are \(Q_i=\{0,1,\ldots,i\}\), with transitions \(q\to q\) for \(x_i=0\) and \(q\to q+1\) for \(x_i=1\).

notation.meaning: count after processing positions 1 through i
reachable count states at layer i

children.title: State-Space Growth
children.top_down_role: Representation-size regimes driven by count ranges and sequential depth.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Space Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts nodes and labeled transition arcs in the full, untruncated layered count-state graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq0}\). In the exact layered count-state representation, layer \(i\) has \(|Q_i|=i+1\) states. Across layers \(0,ldots,n\), the graph has
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{n}|Q_i|=\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2}
\]
state nodes. If the two decisions from each state are represented as separately labeled arcs, the graph has
\[
|A|=\sum_{i=1}^{n}2i=n(n+1)
\]
transition arcs. Thus both counts are \(\Theta(n^2)\). If counts are capped at an upper threshold \(U\), with overflow aggregated when needed, the representation has \(O(nU)\) states and arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact untruncated layered count-state graph has quadratically many state nodes and labeled transition arcs; capping the count at an upper threshold gives order nU size.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq0}\) binary variables are processed without count truncation.
Layer \(i\) contains \(Q_i=\{0,1,\ldots,i\}\), and arcs are counted separately by their binary decision labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The graph has \((n+1)(n+2)/2\) state nodes and \(n(n+1)\) labeled transition arcs, hence \(\Theta(n^2)\) size.

children.title: Sorting-Network Models
children.top_down_role: Comparator-network representations that order binary activity.

knowledge_statements.title: Sorting-Network Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary sorting-network encoding of an at-most-cardinality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). A sorting network is an acyclic composition of binary comparators whose final wires \(y\in\{0,1\}^n\) satisfy \(y_1\geq\cdots\geq y_n\) and are a permutation of \(x\). Each comparator with inputs \(a,b\) and outputs \(c,d\) is encoded by \(c\geq a\), \(c\geq b\), \(d\leq a\), \(d\leq b\), and \(c+d=a+b\), with binary wire variables. Consequently, the constraint \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\leq k\), for \(0\leq k<n\), is represented exactly by the network equations together with \(y_{k+1}=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A comparator network sorts binary inputs; fixing output k+1 to zero exactly enforces that at most k inputs equal one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\leq k\iff y_{k+1}=0\) under the sorting-network constraints.

notation.meaning: sorted output vector in nonincreasing order

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation, comparator encoding, and threshold equivalence are mathematically precise and fit the leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Cardinality-Network Models
children.top_down_role: Comparator networks specialized to support-size restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality-Network Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truncated comparator network for an at-most-cardinality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) and \(0\leq k<n\), a cardinality network computes output wires \(y_1,\ldots,y_{k+1}\) such that \(y_j=1\) exactly when \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\geq j\), without necessarily computing outputs beyond rank \(k+1\). Comparator constraints are imposed on every network gate. The resulting extended formulation together with \(y_{k+1}=0\) projects onto exactly \(\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\leq k\}\). For \(1\leq k\leq n\), a network computing \(y_k\) represents \(\sum_i x_i\geq k\) by imposing \(y_k=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cardinality network computes the threshold outputs needed to encode upper or lower bounds on the number of selected variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_{k+1}=0\iff\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\leq k\).

notation.meaning: threshold output indicating at least j selected inputs

children.title: Comparator Layers
children.top_down_role: Layered organization of comparators within network representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Comparator Layers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel layers of disjoint binary comparators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A comparator layer on \(m\) wires is a set \(L\) of pairwise disjoint unordered index pairs \(\{p,q\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\). After choosing an output orientation for each pair, the comparator on inputs \(u_p,u_q\in\{0,1\}\) produces \(v_p=\max\{u_p,u_q\}\) and \(v_q=\min\{u_p,u_q\}\); every unpaired wire satisfies \(v_r=u_r\). Because no wire occurs in two pairs, all comparators in \(L\) can be evaluated simultaneously. A comparator network is a finite ordered sequence of comparator layers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A comparator layer applies independent compare-exchange gates simultaneously to disjoint pairs of binary wires and copies every unpaired wire.
assumptions_latex: Each wire index occurs in at most one pair of \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_p=\max\{u_p,u_q\}\), \(v_q=\min\{u_p,u_q\}\), and \(v_r=u_r\) for every unpaired \(r\).

children.title: Network-Size Regimes
children.top_down_role: Depth and size tradeoffs across comparator-network designs.

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Size Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic comparator and auxiliary-variable sizes for standard cardinality encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\) binary inputs, a standard constructible sorting network can use \(O(n\log^2 n)\) comparators and depth \(O(\log^2 n)\). Encoding every comparator with a constant number of auxiliary variables and linear constraints therefore gives an extended cardinality formulation of size \(O(n\log^2 n)\). For an at-most-\(k\) constraint, truncated cardinality-network constructions can retain only the first \(k+1\) threshold outputs and attain \(O(n\log^2(k+1))\) comparators for \(1\leq k<n\). These are construction upper bounds, not lower bounds for all comparator networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard full sorting networks yield quasi-linear-log-squared formulations; truncation can reduce size when the cardinality threshold is small.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{\mathrm{sort}}=O(n\log^2 n)\) and \(S_{\mathrm{card}}=O(n\log^2(k+1))\) for the stated constructions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and construction-upper-bound qualification fit the leaf, but the two asymptotic bounds and the encoding-size convention require an inspectable construction source.

children.title: Decision-Diagram Cardinality Models
children.top_down_role: Layered state representations of support-size restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Diagram Cardinality Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Layered count-state diagram for a binary at-most-cardinality set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\leq k\}\), where \(0\leq k\leq n\). Construct a layered acyclic graph with source \((0,0)\), states \((i,s)\) for \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) and \(s\in\{0,\ldots,\min\{i,k\}\}\), and a common sink \(t\). From \((i-1,s)\), include a zero-arc to \((i,s)\), and, when \(s<k\), a one-arc to \((i,s+1)\). Connect every state \((n,s)\) to \(t\). Let \(F\) be the nonnegative unit source-to-sink flow polytope and define \(x_i\) as the total flow on layer-\(i\) one-arcs. Then integral source-to-sink paths correspond bijectively to vectors in \(X\), and \(\operatorname{proj}_x(F)=\operatorname{conv}(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A layered diagram tracks the running number of selections; its paths represent exactly the feasible binary vectors, and its unit-flow formulation projects to their convex hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(F)=\operatorname{conv}\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\leq k\}\).

notation.meaning: state after i decisions with count s

children.title: Generalized Upper-Bound Structures

children.title: Generalized Upper-Bound Sets
children.top_down_role: Partitioned or grouped upper-bound selection structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Upper-Bound Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary grouped-selection form of generalized upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be partitioned into nonempty groups \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\), and let \(u_g\) be nonnegative integers. A binary generalized upper-bound set is
\[X_{\mathrm{GUB}}=\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^{I}:\sum_{i\in G_g}x_i\leq u_g\quad\text{for every }g=1,\ldots,m\right\}.\]
The customary unit-capacity GUB structure has \(u_g=1\) for every group. The defining feature is that the index groups and their bounds are retained as structured data, rather than treated merely as unrelated rows of a linear-inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized upper-bound set partitions binary choices into groups and limits how many variables may be selected in each group.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in X_{\mathrm{GUB}}\iff \sum_{i\in G_g}x_i\leq u_g\) for every \(g\).

children.title: Multiple-Choice Sets
children.top_down_role: Grouped alternatives requiring unique or bounded selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Choice Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Grouped binary alternatives with exact or bounded selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I=G_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}G_m\) and \(x\in\{0,1\}^{I}\). An exact multiple-choice set is
\[X_{\mathrm{MC}}=\left\{x:\sum_{i\in G_g}x_i=1\quad\text{for every }g=1,\ldots,m\right\}.\]
Thus precisely one alternative is selected from each group. Its optional-choice variant replaces equality by \(\sum_{i\in G_g}x_i\leq1\), permitting no selected alternative. More generally, lower and upper group quotas \(\ell_g\leq\sum_{i\in G_g}x_i\leq u_g\) define bounded multiple-choice sets when \(0\leq\ell_g\leq u_g\leq|G_g|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple-choice sets divide alternatives into groups and require exactly one, at most one, or a bounded number of selections per group.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in X_{\mathrm{MC}}\iff\sum_{i\in G_g}x_i=1\) for all \(g\).

notation.meaning: optional lower and upper group quotas

children.title: Generalized Upper-Bound Processing
children.top_down_role: Presolve, branching, and propagation interfaces retaining grouped-choice structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Upper-Bound Processing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact presolve, propagation, and branching operations using group capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a group constraint \(\sum_{i\in G}x_i\leq u\) with binary variables, let \(F=\{i\in G:x_i=1\text{ is fixed}\}\) and \(U\) be the unfixed indices. Feasibility requires \(|F|\leq u\). If \(|F|=u\), propagation fixes \(x_i=0\) for every \(i\in U\). If a lower quota \(\ell\leq\sum_{i\in G}x_i\) is also present and \(|F|+|U|=\ell\), propagation fixes every \(x_i=1\) for \(i\in U\). A group-aware branch partitions remaining admissible selections into exhaustive, disjoint cases while retaining these quota implications in each child.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Group-aware processing detects quota infeasibility, fixes variables when a quota is saturated, and branches on exhaustive grouped alternatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|F|>u\) implies infeasibility; \(|F|=u\) implies \(x_i=0\) for all \(i\in U\).

notation.meaning: indices fixed to one in the group

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Definitions of SOS1 and SOS2
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source's exactly-one convention for SOS1; some solver conventions instead permit at most one nonzero member.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An ordered collection of continuous or integer variables is SOS1 if exactly one member is nonzero. An ordered collection is SOS2 if at most two members are nonzero and, when two are nonzero, their indices are adjacent in the specified ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SOS1 set has exactly one nonzero variable. An SOS2 set has at most two nonzero variables, and any two nonzero variables must be adjacent in the prescribed order.
assumptions_latex: (x_1,\ldots,x_n)\text{ is a collection of continuous or integer variables for SOS1.}
(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\text{ has a specified ordering for SOS2.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{SOS1}:|\{i:x_i\ne0\}|=1;\qquad \operatorname{SOS2}:|\{i:x_i\ne0\}|\le2\ \text{and any two such indices are adjacent}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: SOS1 and SOS2 structures, branching, and interpolation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Special ordered sets as discrete-domain structures and as lambda representations for univariate piecewise-linear interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An SOS1 set x_1,\ldots,x_k permits at most one positive member; in the binary GUB case it is represented by \sum_{j=1}^k x_j=1 with x_j\in\{0,1\}. Given an ordering j_1,\ldots,j_k and a fractional LP solution x^*, an SOS1 branch may use r=\min\{t:\sum_{i=1}^t x_{j_i}^*\geq 1/2\} and partition S into S_1=S\cap\{x:x_{j_i}=0,\ i=1,\ldots,r\} and S_2=S\cap\{x:x_{j_i}=0,\ i=r+1,\ldots,k\}. An SOS2 vector \lambda\in\mathbb R_+^k satisfies \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1 and has at most two nonzero components, which must be adjacent. Thus x=\sum_i\lambda_i x^i and \bar f(x)=\sum_i\lambda_i f(x^i) represent the piecewise-linear interpolant between adjacent breakpoints; separable sums can be represented componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SOS1 permits at most one positive variable; its binary GUB form selects exactly one variable. Ordered SOS1 branching divides the ordered alternatives near one half of the current fractional mass, producing a more balanced partition than ordinary single-variable branching. SOS2 permits at most two nonzero, adjacent lambda variables summing to one, thereby representing interpolation between adjacent breakpoints and extending componentwise to separable functions.
assumptions_latex: x_j\in\{0,1\}\text{ in the stated GUB specialization.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x,\bar f(x))=\left(\sum_i\lambda_i x^i,\sum_i\lambda_i f(x^i)\right)\text{ lies on an adjacent-breakpoint segment, while the ordered SOS1 split partitions the alternatives into two blocks.}

children.title: SOS1 Algebraic Encodings
children.top_down_role: Binary and linear representations of exclusive activity.

knowledge_statements.title: SOS1 Algebraic Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact bounded mixed-integer encoding of at-most-one nonzero component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_i\in[L_i,U_i]\) for \(i\in I\), where \(L_i\leq0\leq U_i\) are finite. The SOS1 condition \(|\{i:x_i\neq0\}|\leq1\) has the exact mixed-integer representation
\[L_i z_i\leq x_i\leq U_i z_i\quad(i\in I),\qquad \sum_{i\in I}z_i\leq1,\qquad z_i\in\{0,1\}.\]
If exactly one member must be active, replace the inequality by \(\sum_i z_i=1\) and additionally impose a valid nonzero-activity condition when selecting \(z_i=1\) must exclude \(x_i=0\); the displayed bounds alone do not enforce that converse implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded SOS1 variables can be linked to binary selectors whose sum is at most one; exact-one activity needs an additional nonzero condition.
assumptions_latex: \(L_i\leq0\leq U_i\) are finite for every \(i\in I\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x\{(x,z):L_i z_i\leq x_i\leq U_i z_i,\sum_i z_i\leq1,z\in\{0,1\}^{I}\}=\{x:|\{i:x_i\neq0\}|\leq1\}\).

notation.meaning: finite valid bounds on the member

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded binary-selector projection is exact and the caveat about exact-one activity is appropriate, but no authoritative SOS1 encoding source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary linear encoding of an SOS1 restriction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The bound-linking formulation guarantees at most one nonzero original variable. Under the source's exactly-one SOS1 convention, an additional condition must prevent the selected variable from taking zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let m_i\le x_i\le M_i and introduce \delta_i\in\{0,1\}. The constraints m_i\delta_i\le x_i\le M_i\delta_i\ (i=1,\ldots,n) and \sum_{i=1}^n\delta_i=1 force exactly one indicator to be active and force x_i=0 whenever \delta_i=0. Hence at most one x_i is nonzero. Exactly one x_i is nonzero if the active indicator also implies x_i\ne0. If x_i\in\{0,1\}, one may take \delta_i=x_i and impose only \sum_i x_i=1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bound-linked binary indicators with exactly one active indicator encode exclusive activity: inactive indicators force their variables to zero, so at most one original variable can be nonzero. Exact nonzero activity additionally requires the selected variable not to equal zero. For binary original variables, the encoding reduces to requiring their sum to equal one.

|\{i:x_i
e0\}|\le1;\quad |\{i:x_i
e0\}|=1\ 	ext{if}\ \delta_i=1\Rightarrow x_i
e0.\quad x_i\in\{0,1\}\Rightarrow \sum_i x_i=1.

children.title: SOS1 Solver Processing

children.title: SOS1 Branching
children.top_down_role: Branching structures that retain SOS1 identity.

knowledge_statements.title: SOS1 Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjunctive branching on a partition of SOS1 members.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an SOS1 index set \(I\), current variable domains, and a partition \(I=P\mathbin{\dot\cup}Q\) with \(P,Q\neq\varnothing\). Create two child nodes. In the first, impose \(x_i=0\) for every \(i\in P\); in the second, impose \(x_i=0\) for every \(i\in Q\). Apply domain propagation in each child and discard an infeasible child. The two child feasible regions cover the current SOS1-feasible region. Continue branch-and-bound until the solver's ordinary termination criterion holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition the SOS1 members and create two children, each forcing one side to zero; together the children cover every SOS1-feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_{\mathrm{SOS1}}\subseteq\{x:x_i=0\ \forall i\in P\}\cup\{x:x_i=0\ \forall i\in Q\}\).

children.title: SOS1 Propagation
children.top_down_role: Domain reduction supported by recognized SOS1 structure.

knowledge_statements.title: SOS1 Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain propagation under exact SOS1 semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input domains \(D_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) for members \(x_i\), \(i\in I\), subject to \(|\{i:x_i
eq0\}|\leq1\). Let \(M=\{i\in I:0
otin D_i\}\). If \(|M|\geq2\), report infeasibility. If \(M=\{j\}\), replace every other domain by \(D_i\leftarrow D_i\cap\{0\}\) for \(i
eq j\), reporting infeasibility if an intersection is empty. If \(M=\varnothing\), no fixing follows from the SOS1 constraint alone. Repeat after subsequent domain changes; implementations using numerical activity tolerances require a separately specified tolerance semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If one SOS1 member cannot be zero, every other member must be zero; if two cannot be zero, the node is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|M|\geq2\Rightarrow\) infeasible, while \(M=\{j\}\Rightarrow D_i\leftarrow D_i\cap\{0\}\) for all \(i\neq j\).

notation.meaning: current domain of SOS1 member i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The domain-propagation algorithm is correct under exact SOS1 semantics and appropriately separates numerical tolerances, but it lacks an authoritative source.

children.title: Solver-Native SOS1 Handling
children.top_down_role: Solver processing paths for preserved SOS1 declarations.

knowledge_statements.title: Solver-Native SOS1 Handling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic requirement for native SOS1 declarations and internal reformulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A native SOS1 declaration on indexed variables \((x_i)_{i\in I}\) specifies the feasible-set condition \(|\{i\in I:x_i\neq0\}|\leq1\), optionally accompanied by distinct weights used to order members for solver processing. Any solver-native propagation, branching scheme, or internal algebraic reformulation is semantically valid only if, under the solver's stated numerical feasibility convention, it preserves this SOS1 feasible set in the original variables. Ordering weights guide processing but do not by themselves alter the exact SOS1 set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A native SOS1 declaration enforces at most one nonzero member; weights may guide processing but should not change the mathematical feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite SOS1 index set.
Any supplied ordering weights are distinct.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_{\mathrm{native}}=\{x:|\{i\in I:x_i\neq0\}|\leq1\}\) under exact semantics.

notation.meaning: original-variable feasible set of the native declaration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact SOS1 semantics and role of ordering weights are plausible and fit the leaf, but native handling, weight requirements, reformulations, and tolerance conventions vary by solver and require solver documentation.

children.title: SOS1 Tolerance Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Near-zero activity regimes affecting SOS1 recognition or enforcement.

knowledge_statements.title: SOS1 Tolerance Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical boundary induced by the solver's activity tolerance for an SOS1 constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb R^n\) and let \(\tau>0\) be the SOS activity tolerance. Define \(A_\tau(x)=\{i:|x_i|>\tau\}\). A tolerance-based SOS1 test accepts \(x\) when \(|A_\tau(x)|\le 1\). Consequently, acceptance need not imply exact SOS1 feasibility: two or more components may be nonzero while satisfying \(|x_i|\le\tau\). Moreover, a perturbation moving any such component across \(\tau\) can change the reported SOS1 status discontinuously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SOS1 test may ignore several nonzero entries below its activity tolerance, and crossing that tolerance can abruptly change feasibility or branching behavior.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) is subject to an SOS1 declaration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|A_\tau(x)|\le1\) does not necessarily imply \(|\{i:x_i\ne0\}|\le1\).

notation.meaning: indices treated as active at tolerance tau

review_flags: solver-specific tolerance conventions require an authoritative source
exact strict-versus-nonstrict activity rule may vary by solver

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, and the mathematical warning is plausible, but the strict activity test and its effect on reported SOS1 status are solver-specific. No source or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Incremental SOS2 Models

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental SOS2 Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental formulation of a univariate piecewise-linear graph over ordered breakpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((a_i,f_i)\), \(i=0,\ldots,m\), be breakpoints with \(a_0<\cdots<a_m\). The piecewise-linear graph is represented by \(0\le\delta_i\le1\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), binaries \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m-1\), and
\[x=a_0+\sum_{i=1}^m(a_i-a_{i-1})\delta_i,\qquad y=f_0+\sum_{i=1}^m(f_i-f_{i-1})\delta_i,\]
\[\delta_{i+1}\le z_i\le\delta_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m-1).\]
At every integer-feasible point, the increments preceding one segment equal one, subsequent increments equal zero, and at most one increment is fractional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordered incremental variables traverse completed segments, one possible partial segment, and then unused segments, yielding the exact piecewise-linear graph.
assumptions_latex: The function is linearly interpolated between consecutive breakpoint values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection onto \((x,y)\) is exactly the piecewise-linear graph through \((a_i,f_i)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the leaf, and the incremental constraints correctly impose completed increments followed by at most one partial increment and then zero increments. An authoritative formulation source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Multiple-Choice SOS2 Models
children.top_down_role: Ordered-segment representations based on explicit segment selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Choice SOS2 Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disaggregated multiple-choice formulation selecting one segment of a piecewise-linear graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For breakpoints \((a_i,f_i)\), \(i=0,\ldots,m\), introduce \(s_i,t_i\ge0\) and \(q_i\in\{0,1\}\) for segments \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Impose
\[s_i+t_i=q_i,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m q_i=1,\]
\[x=\sum_{i=1}^m(a_{i-1}s_i+a_it_i),\qquad y=\sum_{i=1}^m(f_{i-1}s_i+f_it_i).\]
Exactly one segment is selected, and \((s_i,t_i)\) gives its convex interpolation weights. Hence the projection onto \((x,y)\) equals the union of the consecutive line segments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary chooses one breakpoint interval, while two local convex weights interpolate within that interval.
assumptions_latex: The target graph is the union of consecutive line segments joining the breakpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,y)\in\bigcup_{i=1}^m\operatorname{conv}\{(a_{i-1},f_{i-1}),(a_i,f_i)\}\).

notation.meaning: endpoint weights local to segment i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the leaf, and the disaggregated multiple-choice formulation projects onto the stated union of consecutive segments. No supporting formulation source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Segment-Local Variables
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary-variable organization localized to individual ordered segments.

knowledge_statements.title: Segment-Local Variables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local variables used in a disaggregated segment formulation of an SOS2 set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_i=\operatorname{conv}\{v^{i-1},v^i\}\) be segment \(i\), for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Segment-local variables are nonnegative pairs \((s_i,t_i)\) associated only with the endpoints of \(P_i\), together with an activation variable \(q_i\), satisfying \(s_i+t_i=q_i\). The contribution of segment \(i\) to the represented point is \(s_iv^{i-1}+t_iv^i\). Under \(q_i\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\sum_iq_i=1\), variables belonging to every unselected segment vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each segment receives its own endpoint weights; activation forces all weights outside the selected segment to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_i=0\) implies \(s_i=t_i=0\), while \(q_i=1\) makes \((s_i,t_i)\) convex weights on \(P_i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits this leaf, and the stated activation identity gives the claimed behavior for nonnegative local weights. A source with a specific formulation locator is still required.

children.title: SOS2 Extension-Size Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Size and structural-strength regimes across classical SOS2 extensions.

knowledge_statements.title: SOS2 Extension-Size Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size comparison between unary segment extensions and code-based SOS2 extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an SOS2 set on \(m+1\) ordered weights, there are \(m\) admissible consecutive-support segments. A direct segment-selection extension uses \(m\) binary indicators and \(O(m)\) local continuous variables and constraints. An incremental extension uses \(m-1\) binaries and \(O(m)\) continuous variables and constraints. Code-based embedding formulations can use \(r=\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) binary variables, although their auxiliary inequalities and relaxation geometry depend on the chosen codes. Thus fewer binaries do not by themselves imply fewer total rows, nonzeros, or branch-and-bound nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unary and incremental models have linear binary size; encoded embeddings reduce binaries logarithmically but may trade this for constraints and different relaxation behavior.
assumptions_latex: The SOS2 set has \(m\) consecutive segments.
Formulation size counts variables and linear constraints asymptotically in \(m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Binary dimension may decrease from \(\Theta(m)\) to \(\Theta(\log m)\) without guaranteeing universal computational dominance.
review_flags: exact size counts depend on formulation variant

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits the tradeoff leaf. The asymptotic comparison is plausible, but exact variable and row counts depend on the selected formulation variants, and the computational-performance qualification requires comparative evidence. children.title: Logarithmic SOS2 Models
children.top_down_role: Compact SOS2 representations using logarithmic binary descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Logarithmic SOS2 Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-code representation selecting one of the consecutive supports of an SOS2 vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E_i=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^{m+1}:\sum_{j=0}^m\lambda_j=1,\ \lambda_j=0\text{ for }j\notin\{i-1,i\}\}\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Assign distinct codes \(h^i\in\{0,1\}^r\), where \(r=\lceil\log_2m\rceil\), and form
\[Q=\operatorname{conv}\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^m E_i\times\{h^i\}\Bigr).\]
Then imposing \((\lambda,z)\in Q\) and \(z\in\mathbb Z^r\) yields an exact SOS2 formulation: every integer-feasible \(z\) selects one edge \(E_i\). The formulation uses logarithmically many integer coordinates, although an explicit inequality description of \(Q\) is still required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinct binary codes identify the SOS2 segments, so only logarithmically many integer coordinates are needed to select one consecutive support.
assumptions_latex: The codes \(h^1,\ldots,h^m\) are distinct binary vectors of length \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_\lambda\{(\lambda,z)\in Q:z\in\mathbb Z^r\}=\bigcup_{i=1}^mE_i\).

notation.meaning: simplex edge for consecutive indices i-1 and i
binary code assigned to segment i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the leaf. For distinct binary codes, integrality of a point in their convex hull identifies an assigned code, so the exactness claim is mathematically coherent. An authoritative embedding-formulation source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Embedding SOS2 Models
children.top_down_role: SOS2 representations based on codes embedded with ordered alternatives.

assumptions_latex: The sets \(E_i\) are the consecutive simplex edges defining the SOS2 set.

The code set \(H=\{h^1,\ldots,h^m\}\subseteq\mathbb Z^r\) is in convex position and hole-free: every \(h^i\) is a vertex of \(\operatorname{conv}(H)\), and \(\operatorname{conv}(H)\cap\mathbb Z^r=H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{proj}_\lambda\{(\lambda,z)\in Q:z\in\mathbb Z^r\}=\bigcup_{i=1}^mE_i.\]

notation.meaning: integer code assigned to edge i
convex hull of the embedded union

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull embedding of the union of consecutive simplex edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E_1,\ldots,E_m\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+1}\) be the consecutive simplex edges defining an SOS2 set. Assign pairwise distinct codes \(h^1,\ldots,h^m\in\mathbb Z^r\), and write \(H=\{h^1,\ldots,h^m\}\). Assume that every \(h^i\) is a vertex of \(\operatorname{conv}(H)\) and that \(\operatorname{conv}(H)\cap\mathbb Z^r=H\). Define
\[Q=\operatorname{conv}\Bigl(\bigcup_{i=1}^m E_i\times\{h^i\}\Bigr).\]
Then
\[\operatorname{proj}_\lambda\{(\lambda,z)\in Q:z\in\mathbb Z^r\}=\bigcup_{i=1}^mE_i.\]
Thus integrality of the embedded code coordinate enforces membership in a single consecutive edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An embedding attaches a distinct integer code to each SOS2 edge and convexifies the lifted union. When the assigned codes are all vertices of their convex hull and that hull contains no other integer points, integral code coordinates recover exactly one original SOS2 edge.

children.title: Binary-Code Design
children.top_down_role: Code-selection structures governing compact ordered representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary-Code Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Code assignment conditions for exact logarithmic selection of SOS2 segments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(m\) SOS2 segments, a binary-code assignment of length \(r\) is a map \(H:\{1,\ldots,m\}\to\{0,1\}^r\). Exact segment identification requires injectivity:
\[i\ne k\ \Longrightarrow\ H(i)\ne H(k).\]
Consequently, \(2^r\ge m\), so \(r\ge\lceil\log_2m\rceil\). Conversely, an injective assignment exists for \(r=\lceil\log_2m\rceil\). Additional properties, such as small Hamming distance between codes of adjacent segments, may alter the inequality description and branching behavior but are not required merely for unique identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each segment must receive a distinct binary word; the shortest possible word length is the ceiling of the base-two logarithm of the segment count.
assumptions_latex: Codes are binary vectors of a common length \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An injective binary assignment exists if and only if \(r\ge\lceil\log_2m\rceil\).

notation.meaning: binary code assigned to segment i

review_flags: SOS2 embedding context requires a formulation source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits this code-design leaf. The injectivity and minimum code-length claims are precise and correct for unique binary identification, while appropriately distinguishing additional Gray-code properties. A formulation source with a specific locator is missing.

children.title: Gray-Code Embeddings
children.top_down_role: Embedding structures using adjacency-preserving binary codes.

knowledge_statements.title: Gray-Code Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SOS2 embedding whose consecutive segments receive adjacent Gray-code words.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\) be the number of SOS2 segments and \(r=\lceil\log_2m\rceil\). Choose distinct codes \(h^1,\ldots,h^m\in\{0,1\}^r\) satisfying
\[\|h^{i+1}-h^i\|_1=1\qquad(i=1,\ldots,m-1).\]
Embedding segment \(E_i\) as \(E_i\times\{h^i\}\) and taking the convex hull produces a code-based SOS2 model in which adjacent segments differ in exactly one binary coordinate. With the code coordinate constrained to be integral and the embedding hull represented exactly, the projection is the original SOS2 set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gray-code embedding labels neighboring SOS2 segments by binary words differing in one bit while preserving exact segment selection through integrality.
assumptions_latex: The selected sequence contains \(m\) distinct Gray-code words.
The embedded convex hull is represented exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Adjacent segment codes have Hamming distance one, and integer embedded points project onto the SOS2 union.
review_flags: Gray-code SOS2 embedding source not supplied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the leaf. The Gray-code adjacency condition and exact embedded-hull qualification are mathematically coherent, but no authoritative SOS2 embedding source or locator is supplied.

children.title: SOS2 Solver Reliability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Ordered branching, near-zero activity, and tolerance-sensitive adjacency.

children.title: SOS2 Branching
children.top_down_role: Branching structures exploiting the order of SOS2 members.

knowledge_statements.title: SOS2 Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval branching directly on the ordered support of an SOS2 vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given nonnegative ordered weights \(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_m\) with \(\sum_j\lambda_j=1\), compute the tolerance-active set \(A=\{j:\lambda_j>\tau\}\). If \(A\) is contained in two consecutive indices, accept the SOS2 condition. Otherwise choose \(k\) strictly between \(\min A\) and \(\max A\), and create two child nodes:
\[\lambda_j=0\quad(j>k+1),\qquad\text{or}\qquad\lambda_j=0\quad(j<k).\]
The two children cover every exact SOS2 support, overlap on the edge \(\{k,k+1\}\), and reduce the range of potentially active indices. Repeat until the active support is consecutive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branching splits the ordered index range into two overlapping subranges, preserving every consecutive support while shrinking the region containing active weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every exact SOS2-feasible support satisfies at least one child disjunction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the branching leaf, and the overlapping child ranges cover every exact consecutive support. The tolerance-active branching procedure and its relation to actual solver processing are implementation-dependent and require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Near-Zero Activity
children.top_down_role: Small member values that affect perceived SOS2 support.

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Zero Activity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-dependent activity convention for SOS2 weights near zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an ordered SOS2 vector \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^{m+1}\) and tolerance \(\tau\ge0\), define the numerical active set by
\[A_\tau(\lambda)=\{j\in\{0,\ldots,m\}:|\lambda_j|>\tau\}.\]
A component with \(0<|\lambda_j|\le\tau\) is near-zero: it is mathematically nonzero but numerically inactive under this convention. Hence the numerical support \(A_\tau(\lambda)\) may be a strict subset of the exact support \(A_0(\lambda)\), and adjacency tests based on these two supports may disagree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A near-zero SOS2 weight is mathematically nonzero but omitted from the solver's tolerance-based active set, possibly hiding a support violation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_\tau(\lambda)\subseteq A_0(\lambda)\), possibly strictly.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the near-zero-activity leaf, and the set inclusion follows under the explicitly chosen threshold convention. Treating this convention as solver activity behavior requires a solver-specific source and locator.

children.title: Adjacency Tolerances
children.top_down_role: Tolerance regimes governing recognition of adjacent active members.

knowledge_statements.title: Adjacency Tolerances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-based predicate used to test the SOS2 adjacency requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_m\) be ordered weights and let \(A_\tau(\lambda)=\{j:|\lambda_j|>\tau\}\). The tolerance-based SOS2 adjacency condition is
\[|A_\tau(\lambda)|\le2\quad\text{and}\quad \max A_\tau(\lambda)-\min A_\tau(\lambda)\le1,\]
where the second inequality is omitted when \(A_\tau(\lambda)\) is empty. Equivalently, there exists \(k\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\) such that \(A_\tau(\lambda)\subseteq\{k,k+1\}\), with singleton endpoint supports also allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After discarding weights no larger than the activity tolerance, all remaining nonzeros must occupy at most two consecutive ordered positions.
assumptions_latex: The indices \(0,\ldots,m\) carry the declared SOS2 order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The numerically active support lies in one consecutive index pair.
review_flags: solver-specific strictness and scaling rules require sourcing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the adjacency-tolerance leaf, and the predicate correctly characterizes containment in a consecutive index pair under the stated convention. Strictness, scaling, and numerical activity rules vary by solver, and no authoritative source or locator is supplied.

children.title: SOS2 Numerical Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Numerical conditions that compromise ordered-set interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: SOS2 Numerical Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-induced loss of exact SOS2 support semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^n_+\) have an SOS2 restriction in the order \(1,\ldots,n\), and let a solver classify \(\lambda_i\) as inactive whenever \(\lambda_i\leq\tau\), where \(\tau>0\). If \(i<j-1\), \(0<\lambda_i\leq\tau\), and \(\lambda_j>\tau\), the solver-observed support may omit \(i\) and appear SOS2-feasible although the exact support contains the nonadjacent indices \(i\) and \(j\). Consequently, exact SOS2 semantics are not numerically certified unless activity tolerances, coefficient scaling, and post-solve support checks distinguish every materially positive component from zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver may overlook a small positive coefficient and accept an exactly nonadjacent SOS2 support; scaling and post-solve checks are therefore necessary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{supp}(\lambda)\text{ can violate SOS2 while the tolerance-filtered support satisfies SOS2.}\)
review_flags: solver-specific tolerance semantics require an authoritative numerical-reliability source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure mechanism is plausible and fits the failure-boundary container, but the solver activity rule and resulting certification claim require an authoritative numerical-reliability or solver-documentation source.

children.title: Generalized Ordered-Support Sets
children.top_down_role: Ordered support restrictions extending the standard SOS1 and SOS2 families.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Ordered-Support Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered supports specified by an explicit admissible family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an ordered index set \(I=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and a family \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq 2^I\) of admissible supports. The generalized ordered-support set generated by \(\mathcal{A}\) is
\[S(\mathcal{A})=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq A\text{ for some }A\in\mathcal{A}\}.\]
If \(\mathcal{A}\) consists of all singletons, this gives an SOS1 restriction; if it consists of all adjacent pairs together with their subsets, it gives an SOS2 restriction. Other choices encode bounded consecutive blocks or prescribed ordered support patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An admissible family of index subsets defines which ordered support patterns are allowed, including SOS1, SOS2, and longer consecutive blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in S(\mathcal{A})\iff \exists A\in\mathcal{A}:\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq A.\)
review_flags: terminology and intended generalization require a direct special-ordered-set source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The admissible-support construction is mathematically coherent, but no source establishes that “generalized ordered-support set” is the intended SOS generalization or supports the claimed examples.

children.title: Disjunctive Model Architecture
children.top_down_role: Model structures whose feasible regions are organized as unions of alternatives.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Model classifications and outer convexification for mixed-integer control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-model and discrete-event representations for mixed-integer optimal control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume appropriate boundary conditions and fixed controls \((u,v)\) uniquely determine the differential-algebraic state \(x\). An explicit ODE model has
\[
\dot x(t)=f(x(t),u(t),v(t))\quad\text{for a.e. }t\in[t_0,t_f].
\]
A DAE model also contains algebraic variables and constraints, while a PDE model has more than one independent variable. If \(\Omega=\{v^1,\ldots,v^{n_\omega}\}\), outer convexification introduces controls \(\omega_i(t)\) satisfying
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n_\omega}F[x,u,v^i]\omega_i(t)=0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{n_\omega}\omega_i(t)=1.
\]
With \(\omega(t)\in\{0,1\}^{n_\omega}\), this is bijective with finite-valued controls \(v(t)\in\Omega\); the relaxation uses \(\omega(t)\in[0,1]^{n_\omega}\). State-dependent switches have the form \(F_i[x,u,v]=0\) when \(\sigma_i(x(t))\ge0\), and Boolean activation variables can express switching alternatives as a disjunctive program. Multistage models use equations \(F_i[x,u,v]=0\) on intervals \([t_i,t_{i+1}]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed controls and suitable boundary conditions, the state is assumed uniquely determined. Models may be classified as ODE, DAE, or PDE systems and may include outer-convexified finite controls, state-dependent switches, Boolean or disjunctive activation, multistage dynamics, unstable dynamics, or network structure. Outer convexification represents each finite control value by a one-hot binary control and relaxes the binary vector to simplex-valued weights.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is uniquely determined by fixed }(u,v)\text{ and appropriate boundary conditions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v(t)\in\Omega\ \longleftrightarrow\ \omega(t)\in\{0,1\}^{n_\omega},\ \mathbf 1^T\omega(t)=1;\qquad \omega(t)\in[0,1]^{n_\omega}\text{ gives the relaxed representation.}

children.top_down_role: Finite unions distinguished by the number and interaction of their alternatives.

children.title: Two-Term Disjunctions
children.top_down_role: Binary unions serving as elementary disjunctive building blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Term Disjunctions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary union of explicitly described feasible alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(D_1,D_2\subseteq X\) be sets described by their respective local constraints. A two-term disjunction imposes
\[x\in D_1\ \lor\ x\in D_2,\]
equivalently \(x\in D_1\cup D_2\). With Boolean selectors \(Y_1,Y_2\), exclusive selection is represented logically by \(Y_1\lor Y_2\), \(\neg(Y_1\land Y_2)\), and implications \(Y_i\Rightarrow x\in D_i\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\). The union itself permits points lying in both terms unless exclusivity is separately imposed on the selectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-term disjunction requires a point to satisfy at least one of two local feasible systems; exclusive selection is an additional logical condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ satisfies the disjunction}\iff x\in D_1\cup D_2.\)

children.title: Multiple-Term Disjunctions
children.top_down_role: Unions with several explicitly selectable alternatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Term Disjunctions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite union with one or more selectable alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) with \(m\geq 2\), and let \(D_k\subseteq X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be the feasible set of alternative \(k\). A multiple-term disjunction imposes
\[\bigvee_{k\in K}[x\in D_k],\]
which is equivalent to \(x\in\bigcup_{k\in K}D_k\). Boolean selectors \(Y_k\) may satisfy \(\bigvee_{k\in K}Y_k\) together with \(Y_k\Rightarrow x\in D_k\). If \(y_k\in\{0,1\}\) is the binary encoding of \(Y_k\), then \(\sum_{k\in K}y_k=1\) enforces exactly one selected alternative, which is an additional selection convention when the sets overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple-term disjunction is a finite union of local feasible sets; exactly-one selection is an additional condition and can be imposed on binary selector encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ satisfies the disjunction}\iff x\in\bigcup_{k\in K}D_k.\)

notation.meaning: binary encoding of the Boolean selector

children.title: Interacting Disjunction Systems
children.top_down_role: Models formed by intersections of multiple unions.

knowledge_statements.title: Interacting Disjunction Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersection of finite unions sharing variables or logic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\) index disjunctions and let \(D_{qk}\subseteq X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be alternative \(k\in K_q\) of disjunction \(q\). An interacting disjunction system has feasible set
\[F=G\cap\bigcap_{q\in Q}\left(\bigcup_{k\in K_q}D_{qk}\right),\]
where \(G\subseteq X\) contains global constraints. The disjunctions interact when their sets involve shared components of \(x\), their selectors satisfy cross-disjunction logical propositions, or both. In general, \(F\) is not obtained by solving each union independently because global and shared-variable constraints couple the selected alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Several disjunctions interact through shared variables, global constraints, or cross-disjunction logic, so their alternatives cannot generally be selected independently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=G\cap\bigcap_{q\in Q}\bigcup_{k\in K_q}D_{qk}.\)
